graphify.summary: Graphify (now Graphify-Labs/graphify; PyPI graphifyy; v0.9.108 on 2026-11-12; 146,932 stars in about 7 months; Apache-2.0) builds a NetworkX property graph in two layers: a deterministic tree-sitter code layer (files, classes, functions, imports, calls, inheritance, SQL schema) and an optional model-read layer over docs, PDFs and images (concept nodes, rationale text, cross-document and doc-to-code edges). It is not temporal, not a TKG, not a graph database, and stores no summaries (a summaries RFC is unmerged). Query is lexical seed-finding (substring, trigram, IDF on labels) followed by breadth-first expansion cut at a 2,000-token budget; clustering is Leiden with Louvain fallback; a report file lists god nodes, surprising links and communities; an always-on CLAUDE.md block and advisory hooks tell the agent to query first. The 71.5x headline is a ratio of two estimates (whole 52-file corpus, about 123,488 tokens, mostly five PDFs, against about 1,726 tokens per graph answer, five generic questions), with no correctness check, run once by the maintainer in April 2026; the same corpus code-only gives 8.8x; a later contributor fix says it was never re-run. The README's lead numbers are for conversational memory (LOCOMO, LongMemEval), and the one code-agent number is 6 questions on ERPNext (82.0% vs 70.8%, no interval, harness not public). Independent measurements are mostly null or negative on code for a strong model, and the one clear positive is doc-versus-code questions, which is the model-read layer the owner's finished test did not include.

findings.claim: The 71.5x figure compares the whole 52-file corpus put in context (about 123,488 tokens, estimated as words x 4/3) with the average size of one graph-traversal answer (about 1,726 tokens) for five generic questions. No answer was graded and no selective-search baseline was used. On the same corpus, code only, the ratio is 8.8x.
findings.evidence: worked/karpathy-repos/review.md: corpus 52 files, about 92,616 words, 123,488 naive tokens; avg query 1,726; 71.5x; code-only 16,997 vs 1,929 tokens = 8.8x. graphify/benchmark.py computes corpus_words*100//75 and, if no word count is given, nodes*50. how-it-works.md lists 5.4x for a 4-file corpus and about 1x for a 6-file one and says six files already fit in a context window.
findings.how_measured: By the maintainer, once, 2026-04-04; ratio of two token estimates (characters/4 for the answer, words x 4/3 for the corpus). No agent run; no correctness metric. The sibling httpx review is labelled an analytical simulation by a model without running code.

findings.claim: The 71.5x was not re-run after the benchmark's answer-side counting was changed in v0.9.87, and the ratio is driven by the 2,000-token cap against a growing corpus. The project's own benchmark command still does not measure whether answers are right.
findings.evidence: PR 4348 (shipped v0.9.87 per maintainer): 'I did not re-run it because the corpus is not in the repo'; the benchmark's own output moved from 10.2x to 32.4x (requests), 10.8x to 113.3x (flask), 78.7x to 153.6x (pytest), 11.0x to 1,893.5x (django). Issue 4341 'graphify benchmark measures answer size but never whether the answer is right' is open.
findings.how_measured: Contributor reran the project's benchmark script on four public repositories before and after a code fix.

findings.claim: Graphify's current README lead numbers (recall@10 0.497, QA 45.3%, LongMemEval-S 76%) are for conversational memory, not code. Graph expansion adds about 2.6 points over seed-only retrieval on 300 questions, within one binomial standard error (about 2.9 points, my arithmetic). The benchmark arm uses a local embedder and hybrid retrieval while the README says no embeddings. The harness (memory/, crosstool/) is not in the public repository.
findings.evidence: BENCHMARKS.md: LOCOMO n=300: graphify 45.3%, hybrid RRF 43.3%, dense 41.3%, BM25 31.3%, mem0 27.3%, supermemory 49.7%; seed-only ablation 42.7%. Judge Kimi K2.6, 90.6% agreement with a second judge, kappa 0.81. Repository tree at v8 (1,311 entries) has no crosstool or memory directory.
findings.how_measured: Maintainers' own harness with competitors run as adapters, shared model and grader, one repetition, key-fact coverage graded by a model.

findings.claim: The only code-agent result in the project's materials is 6 questions on ERPNext (about 1M lines): key-fact coverage 82.0% with one graph tool vs 70.8% for grep and read, at about 140K tokens per query, Opus-class agent capped at 14 turns. No interval, no baseline token figure, harness not public.
findings.evidence: BENCHMARKS.md 'Results: code intelligence'. A difference of 11.2 points on 6 questions is about one question's worth (my arithmetic).
findings.how_measured: Maintainers; fixed agent; key-fact coverage graded by a model; n=6.

findings.claim: Independent retrieval check on 177 SWE-bench Lite issues: graphify's query_graph showed the right file first in 25% of cases (first 5: 38%, anywhere: 62%) against BM25 over .py files at 32% first, 64% in first 5, 92% in top 50.
findings.evidence: Issue 4341 tables, graphify 0.9.85, MCP defaults (BFS, depth 3, about 2,000 tokens), nine Python repositories each built at the commit of the issue; question = issue title; right answer = files the real fix changed.
findings.how_measured: Contributor rohit-jsfreaky; known-answer public benchmark; file localisation only, no agent.

findings.claim: Controlled agent benchmark (940 Claude Code runs, 105 tasks, one synthetic SaaS, 477 code files plus 139 design docs): on Sonnet 5 code tasks graphify changes nothing measurable (tokens +32k [-8k,+75k], accuracy 78% vs 84%; against a no-subagent baseline +107k [+38k,+180k] tokens). It helps a weak explorer (Haiku 4.5: -119k tokens [-245k,-12k], 82% vs 80%) and doc-and-code questions (Sonnet 5: 80% vs 70%, cost -0.084 USD [-0.180,-0.005]); in the planted doc-vs-code contradiction hunt it found 4 of 4 (F1 0.94) vs 2 of 4 (0.68).
findings.evidence: Author's caveats: one corpus, one repetition per task, intervals resample tasks, subagent tokens uncounted (inflates graphify cost on code tasks), affected/god-nodes/save-result/reflect called zero times, strict first-read block never fired in 45 runs. Graph v1 code-only: 2,545 nodes, 10,202 edges, 4.6 s, no model; v2 with doc extraction: about 7 USD of Sonnet subagent calls.
findings.how_measured: Independent author; real headless agent sessions; set-F1 vs key, blind model judge, or hidden tests; bootstrap intervals over tasks; all transcripts published.

findings.claim: Smaller independent tests mostly show no session-level saving: two agents x 5 questions x 2 repos (tokens 79.6k vs 53.1k and 83.5k vs 62.1k, more tool calls, agent re-read files because 82% of nodes and edges had no source line, one fabricated line citation); six production feature sessions (cost 60.28 vs 47.83, 25.60 vs 27.06, 10.55 vs 12.85 USD per round, blind quality 44/50 vs 45/50, 46 grep calls vs 18 graphify calls); a 60-session audit with 0 graph calls and about 1,500 ignored hook reminders; a V-library 8-question test with 67.5 vs 68.5 of 69 items and 361k vs 414k weighted input tokens.
findings.evidence: Issues 3307/3308 (graphify 0.9.53); KubeBlogs three-round study (n=1 per arm per round; arm-to-cost mapping inferred by the page reader); rentierdigital 14-day audit of two projects; quaesitor-scientiam PR 100 (two runs per tool, blind key).
findings.how_measured: Third parties; small n, mostly single runs; authors call them directional or anecdotal.

findings.claim: The query engine is lexical seed-finding plus graph expansion, not graph-native ranking: nodes scored by substring, trigram and IDF match on labels and paths; top few become seeds; BFS or DFS to a depth with a token cut; the skill adds a model-run vocabulary-expansion step because the engine has no stemming, synonyms or cross-language match. No embeddings or personalised PageRank in the query path.
findings.evidence: serve.py functions _score_query, _pick_seeds, _bfs, _subgraph_to_text, _query_graph_text; references/query.md Step 0.
findings.how_measured: Read the current source; not executed.

findings.claim: Graph type: NetworkX multigraph saved as node-link JSON with arc-order direction, hyperedges in a side list, node file_type in {code, document, paper, image, rationale, concept}, edge confidence EXTRACTED (1.0) / INFERRED (0.55 to 0.95 rubric) / AMBIGUOUS (0.1 to 0.3). Cross-file code edges from the parser's resolver are tagged INFERRED. No validity intervals, no history, no invalidation through the graph; cache invalidation is per file by content hash (plus extraction-prompt hash for model results). Temporal sub-suite in the benchmark is 689 separate weekly AST snapshots with only node and edge counts reported. Summaries exist only as an unmerged RFC.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md, how-it-works.md, extraction-spec.md, node-summaries-rfc.md; search of serve.py, report.py, README and ARCHITECTURE for valid-from, as-of, bitemporal, invalidation found only cache comments.

findings.claim: What an installed agent is told to do: run graphify query before the first grep or source read, read raw files only for located lines, read the report only for broad review, run graphify update after edits. On Claude Code and Gemini CLI an advisory PreToolUse hook nudges (capped at 5 per session); strict mode denies the first raw Read/Grep once per session unless a graph query occurred in the last 30 minutes. Other platforms get an instruction file only. Measured behaviour: advisory text was often ignored.
findings.evidence: always_on/claude-md.md, skills/claude/references/hooks.md, README 'Make your assistant always use the graph'; behavioural counts in graphify-bench, KubeBlogs and the 60-session audit.
findings.how_measured: Read source; behaviour from third-party counts.

findings.claim: Build and data cost: code is parsed locally at zero model tokens (4.6 s for 477 files in the independent bench). Every uncached non-code file is read in full by a model: about 7 USD of Sonnet subagents for 139 markdown files (261k words) in the independent bench; a blog reports about 240k tokens (range 200k to 280k) for a 140-file project and about 40k for a 3-file update, and that graphify's own cost tracker reported zero. No published figure for a 1,000-file mixed repository. Code never leaves the machine; documents, PDFs and images go to the host model or the configured backend (Kimi routes to Moonshot servers in China); no telemetry; local query log unless disabled; Cloud is hosted by the vendor.
findings.evidence: README Privacy section; how-it-works.md three passes; graphify-bench graph v1/v2 lines; exchangepedia build-cost section.
findings.how_measured: Maintainer statements plus two third-party builds; no controlled cost study.

findings.claim: Adoption and project facts: 146,932 stars, 14,093 forks, 423 watchers, 1,639 open issues and pull requests; created 2026-04-03; roughly one release per day (v0.9.108 on 2026-11-12, 276 PyPI releases); Apache-2.0; Python 3.10 to 3.14; wheel 1.9 MB, sdist 3.4 MB; core deps networkx, numpy, rapidfuzz, pyyaml, tree-sitter plus about 25 grammars. The organisation sells a hosted product (Graphify Cloud, claims '80% fewer tokens' with no stated method) and the founder sells a book; the README is partly marketing. Star count is attention and adoption, not an effect size.

findings.how_measured: Read from live API on 2026-11-13.

what_it_means_for_the_test: The contrast 'our experiments failed but graphify looks good' is not like for like. Graphify's lead numbers are a whole-corpus-in-context baseline with no correctness check (71.5x), a conversational-memory task (LOCOMO), and 6 questions on one repository (ERPNext). Its independent controlled code results are mostly null or negative on a strong model, which agrees with the finished test (typed store slightly better than scripted search; graph-native step +0.015 with an interval including zero).

The owner is right that the finished test left out the one layer graphify adds: model-read meaning over documents, doc-to-code links, and an always-on pointer. The only independent positive result found (doc-versus-code questions, Sonnet 5 80% vs 70%, contradiction hunt 4 of 4 vs 2 of 4, from graphify-bench) sits in that layer. A next test should include a model-extracted doc-and-code layer, with its build cost counted, and an agent in the loop.

The owner's 31-token versus 695-token answer-size comparison is the same kind of quantity as graphify's token-reduction ratio, and is subject to the same limitation: it says nothing about whether an agent given a typed query program finds the right query to ask. The independent agent runs show the dominant cost is behaviour (agents ignore the tool, re-read files after a graph answer), so an agent-in-the-loop arm with usage counted across subagents is what would separate the claims.

Graphify is not a temporal knowledge graph: no validity intervals, no history, per-file hash caching. Nothing in its evidence speaks for or against temporal knowledge graphs. If temporal graphs are to be tested, graphify cannot serve as the evidence or as a stand-in arm; the closest in-graph time signal in the owner's graph is git co-change, which graphify lacks (open PR only).

Graphify's retrieval is lexical seeds plus breadth-first expansion; its code layer is a parser-built typed graph, the same family as the tested graph. An established-tool arm for the next round could be graphify run as shipped (code layer, then with doc extraction) against the same tasks, scored for correctness, with the same agent and with usage counted across subagents. Its `affected` command is the direct analogue of the changed-file recall task, and no public measurement of it exists (graphify-bench called it zero times).

Score for correctness in any graphify arm: the project's own benchmark command measures only answer size, and the maintainers' tracker has an open request to add correctness. Use known-answer sets (the owner's held-out commits; a SWE-bench-style localisation check as in issue 4341) so a smaller answer cannot be mistaken for a better one.
could_not_verify: The memory/ and crosstool/ harnesses behind the README numbers are not in the public repository; the ERPNext questions, keys and baseline token counts could not be read, so 82.0% vs 70.8% cannot be reproduced.
What the graph contains in the LOCOMO and LongMemEval arms, and why a local embedder and hybrid retrieval are used when the README says no embeddings and no vector store.
Any independent reproduction of 71.5x on the Karpathy corpus; none found, and the maintainers' later benchmark fix says the old figure was not re-run.
Whether the 146,932 stars are organic; not investigated, no evidence either way.
Whether graphify extracts code-to-table read and write edges (it advertises SQL schema, foreign keys and joins).

Installed size on disk; the model-token cost of building a 1,000-file mixed repository (only two third-party data points for about 140 files); the behaviour and method of the hosted Graphify Cloud and its '80% fewer tokens' claim; undisclosed network calls (code not audited).

The dev.to review returned 404; model names such as 'Sonnet 5' and 'Opus 5.5' in third-party write-ups could not be confirmed. I did not run graphify; all figures are readings of sources, except my own arithmetic (binomial standard error about 2.9 points at n=300; six-question sensitivity; words-to-token estimates).

temporal.summary: A temporal knowledge graph gives an agent nothing that one snapshot per commit cannot answer about a past state. The snapshot at commit K is the "as of K" view. What an interval store adds is economy, cross-time questions in one pass, and one real primitive: a derived conclusion that carries the set of facts it rests on and stays valid until one of them changes. That primitive is the build-systems idea (verifying traces, early cutoff), not a knowledge-graph novelty. The owner is right that the finished test never tried cached conclusions, because its facts were parser-extracted and cost no model tokens. He is wrong that published temporal-graph results are evidence for the code case. They are conversation-memory benchmarks, mostly self-reported, against a full-context baseline. The one independent benchmark of contradictory updates (MemoryAgentBench) ranked Zep lowest of all methods tried. The independent code-agent evidence on cached conclusions is negative or flat. I found no controlled study that caches LLM-made conclusions about code, invalidates them by dependency, and measures agent tokens and success. That gap is where the next test should go.

findings.claim: Zep's headline result is a context reduction against a full-conversation baseline, with a modest accuracy gain, and no plain-RAG row.
findings.evidence: LongMemEval (about 115k tokens per conversation): average context 1.6k tokens against 115k (about 72 times fewer). Accuracy 63.8% against 55.4% (gpt-4o-mini) and 71.2% against 60.2% (gpt-4o), i.e. +8.4 and +11.0 points. The paper's '15.2%' and '18.5%' are relative gains. Latency 3.2 s against 31.3 s, but Zep's figure includes a laptop-to-AWS network hop the baseline did not have. Knowledge-update, the category closest to invalidation: 76.9% to 74.4% (gpt-4o-mini, a drop) and 78.2% to 83.3% (gpt-4o). The authors call the DMR benchmark inadequate because conversations fit in context.
findings.how_measured: By Zep's own authors, Dec 2024 to Jan 2025, gpt-4o as judge, baseline = whole conversation in context. No measured precision or recall for contradiction detection.

findings.claim: Even in the memory vendors' own tables, memory systems trade a few judge points for large token and latency savings against full context, and the vendors dispute each other's numbers.
findings.evidence: Mem0 paper on LoCoMo (about 26,031 tokens per conversation): full context 72.90 judge score; Mem0g 68.44 at 3,616 context tokens; Mem0 66.88 at 1,764 tokens; Zep 65.99 at 3,911 tokens; best plain RAG 60.97. p95 total latency: Mem0 1.44 s, Zep 2.93 s, full context 17.1 s. Mem0 reports a stored Zep graph of over 600k tokens per conversation against 26k raw. Zep replies with a corrected 75.14 +/- 0.17 and says Mem0 mis-ran Zep (timestamps in text, wrong user role, sequential searches); it also says full context scores about 73%. Mem0's re-run put Zep at 58.44% (secondary report, not read at source). No resolution found.
findings.how_measured: Self-run by each vendor, LLM judge, 10 runs for Mem0's table, baselines full context and RAG at several chunk sizes.

findings.claim: The benchmarks behind the memory-system numbers are themselves unreliable, and a grep-style agent matched or beat the graph memories on their own benchmark.
findings.evidence: LoCoMo audit: 99 of 1,540 answer-key entries (6.4%) wrong, so the ceiling is about 93.6%; the judge accepted 62.81% of deliberately vague on-topic wrong answers and 10.61% of specific wrong answers. LoCoMo and LongMemEval both fit in current context windows. Letta's agent with grep, search_files, open and close scored 74.0% on LoCoMo with gpt-4o-mini against the 68.5% Mem0 reported for its best graph variant.
findings.how_measured: Audit by an unnamed or lightly identified author with no independent confirmation found; Letta result by a competing memory vendor.

findings.claim: Independent evidence on contradictory updates is poor for memory systems that use an LLM to invalidate.
findings.evidence: MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation (newer fact must win, contexts 6k to 262k tokens, 100 questions per variant), single-hop / multi-hop accuracy in percent: GPT-4o long context 60/5; HippoRAG-v2 54/5; BM25 48/3; Cognee 28/3; MemGPT 28/3; Mem0 18/2; GraphRAG 14/2; Zep 7/3. All methods at most 7% on multi-hop. Caveats: recency is encoded as a serial number in the text, not as the timestamp field Zep expects; the paper does not describe vendor-recommended configuration or explain the low scores.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.05257v2 (read; UC San Diego, ICLR 2026 poster)
findings.how_measured: Independent group, same backbone (gpt-4o-mini) and same chunk size across memory agents, long-context and plain-retrieval baselines.

findings.claim: In Graphiti's code, invalidation is decided by a small LLM over embedding-similar candidates, with no semantic check afterwards.
findings.evidence: A new fact is embedded; duplicate candidates are limited to the same two endpoints, but contradiction candidates are any semantically close edge in the group; a 'small' model returns index lists of duplicates and contradictions; invalid_at on the older fact is set to the new fact's valid_at only when windows overlap and the older started earlier; candidates with a missing date are skipped; out-of-range indices are logged and ignored. The README states temporal facts, episodes, hybrid retrieval, Neo4j, FalkorDB, Neptune and a deprecated Kuzu driver, 32.8k stars, Apache-2.0, no retrieval benchmark of its own, and warns that smaller models may cause ingestion failures.
findings.how_measured: Reading current source and README. Stars are adoption, not effect.
findings.strength: strong for what the code does; says nothing about how accurate it is

findings.claim: Independent code-agent evidence on cached or summarised conclusions is negative or flat.
findings.evidence: VibeMemBench (111 targets, 90 repositories, executable tests, matched memory-off baselines): 11 of 12 pairings of solver and memory system (Mem0, SimpleMem, MemoryOS, A-MEM) did not beat memory off, e.g. deepseek-v4-pro 67.1% off against Mem0 62.8% (-4.3 points); 160 of 231 failures were in the form of the stored record, not retrieval. ETH AGENTS.md study (138 instances, 300 SWE-bench Lite tasks, 4 agent and model pairs): LLM-written repository context files changed resolution by -0.5% and -2% (not significant) and raised cost about 20% to 23% (significant); repository overviews did not help find the files. SWE Context Bench (99 related tasks): resolution no experience 26.26%, oracle summary reuse 34.34%, free summary reuse 22.22% (below baseline); cost per instance $0.79 none, $0.77 oracle summary, $0.85 free summary. None of the three studies staleness.
findings.how_measured: Resolution by executable tests against a no-memory or no-context baseline; cost from agent logs. Python-heavy, small n, one sample per instance in the ETH study.

findings.claim: The only code-specific token-saving number for a graph-plus-index layer is self-reported, small, and comes with a resolution drop it cannot resolve.
findings.evidence: ContextSniper (not temporal): 50 SWE-bench Lite tasks per host agent. OpenClaw: tokens 1.36M to 0.66M per task (-51.5%), cost -36.4%, resolution 26.0% to 24.0%. Claude Code: tokens -38.9%, cost $15.09 to $10.97, resolution 32.0% to 30.0%. No confidence intervals; authors say repair-success conclusions are not firm. It keeps the index fresh with hooks and by reconciling against the working tree with repository diffs.
findings.how_measured: By the tool's own authors against each host agent's default tools.

findings.claim: Temporal-validity results on code are single-author or small-benchmark and use facts already in triple form, which removes the hard extraction step.
findings.evidence: MemStrata (deterministic supersession of (subject, relation, object) triples): 130 clean transitions mined from 707 SWE-bench issues; accuracy 0.91 against 0.57 to 0.59 for plain RAG; plain RAG served the superseded value 36 to 38% of the time, MemStrata about 0%. Only about 18% of real fixes were clean transitions. VersionRAG (versioned documents): 90% against 58% (plain RAG) and 64% (GraphRAG) on the authors' own 100 questions; 97% fewer indexing tokens than GraphRAG. AgenticSZZ (temporal graph of commits for bug-inducing commit search): F1 0.47 to 0.79, up to 34% over prior methods; a history-forensics task, not context retrieval.
findings.how_measured: Authors' own benchmarks; baselines plain RAG, RAG with LLM reranker, GraphRAG.

findings.claim: Dependency-tracked caching with early cutoff is the well-understood, production-proven form of 'cached conclusions with invalidation', and Glean is the nearest existing design to facts valid per file with derived facts that carry their dependencies.
findings.evidence: Skyframe: bottom-up invalidation, change pruning when a rebuilt value is unchanged, unregistered dependencies cause incorrect incremental builds. Salsa: per-input changed-revision, backdating, durability. rustc red-green: result-hash comparison stops propagation. Glean: facts labelled by unit, stacked databases hide changed units, ownership propagates so no visible fact points to a hidden one, a derived fact is visible only when all its sources are; about 2 to 3% indexing overhead for Python, about 7% larger database, typical queries under 10% slower, incremental derivation only for some query kinds. Cursor re-embeds only chunks under changed Merkle-tree branches and caches embeddings by chunk content.
findings.source: https://bazel.build/reference/skyframe ; https://salsa-rs.github.io/salsa/reference/algorithm.html ; https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/queries/incremental-compilation.html ; https://glean.software/blog/incremental ; https://cursor.com/blog/secure-codebase-indexing (all read); trace-type definitions from slides https://www.sambuz.com/doc/build-systems-ppt-presentation-809664
findings.how_measured: Documentation and engineering posts by the systems' builders; Glean's overhead numbers are Meta's own. No agent-token measurements in any of them. The Build Systems a la Carte PDF could not be read.
findings.strength: strong as engineering description; no token evidence

findings.claim: graphify, the tool the owner cites, is not a temporal graph and its published benchmarks are self-reported on small samples, mostly conversation memory.
findings.evidence: README: tree-sitter parsing with no model for code, model pass for documents and images, edges tagged EXTRACTED or INFERRED, incremental re-extraction of changed files, git hooks, no validity or history model. Its stated benchmarks: LoCoMo n=300 recall at 10 of 0.497 against Mem0 0.048; LongMemEval-S n=50 76% accuracy tied with dense RAG; ERPNext n=6 82.0% key-fact coverage against 70.8% for grep and read. The '80%' token figure appears only in cloud-product promotion with no baseline. 146.9k stars is adoption, not effect.
findings.how_measured: Self-reported by the project; judge blind-validated against a second judge (90.6% agreement, kappa 0.81) per README.

findings.claim: A full rebuild of the facts is cheap in this repository, so caching deterministic extraction saves seconds, not tokens; the only place token saving could come from is cached conclusions that are expensive to derive.
findings.evidence: 190 per-parent builds: median 10,847 edges, p50 5.3 s per build with three concurrent (4.5 to 7 s alone), 778 MB total (about 4.1 MB per commit), byte-identical on rebuild, cache keyed on commit plus an extractor version hash. Typed query 31 tokens against about 695 tokens for scripted search on the structured questions (from the task description).
findings.how_measured: The finished test's own build log; per-kind token numbers in build-e/result.json were not re-read in this lane.

what_it_means_for_the_test: Do not cite published temporal-graph numbers as support for the code case. They compare to full context on chat transcripts and are mostly vendor-reported; the independent tests (MemoryAgentBench, VibeMemBench, the ETH AGENTS.md study) do not show those systems or LLM-written summaries helping on updates or repository tasks.

The owner's cached-conclusions idea is untested by the finished test, not refuted by it. The finished test used deterministic parser facts that cost no tokens, so there was nothing expensive to cache. State that plainly in any report.

Run the smallest honest test in two steps, no model first. Test 1: replay the 190 existing per-commit snapshots; for the 50 structured questions plus about 200 mechanically generated ones, record each answer's dependency set, apply policies (no cache, whole-repo, file-hash, fact-level, fact-level with early cutoff, mtime-style) and compare with the answer recomputed at the next commit. Report stale-served rate (must be zero), avoidable-recompute rate, and hit rate by age. Test 2: price the hits using the measured 695 versus 31 tokens on the 75 held-out commits to get an upper bound on saving, and compare it with the session's total token cost.

Only if Test 1 and Test 2 are positive, run an agent pilot of 24 to 30 fix commits with four matched arms: grep, grep plus typed queries on the current snapshot, plus cached conclusions with invalidation, and plus the same cached conclusions with no invalidation as the stale control. Score tests passed and total tokens including prompt-prefix re-reads. Score stale uses as wrong and treat the result as a pilot.

Put the cache key (commit, extractor version, query-program version, and for any model-made conclusion the model and prompt version) in the protocol, record negative dependencies ('no other caller') explicitly, and handle the uncommitted working tree by content hash or diff, since commits form a DAG and an agent's edits match no snapshot.

Add deterministic validity checks where they are free: close a doc-to-file citation edge when the target file disappears. The earlier research recorded 517 of 1,268 backticked file names in docs that do not resolve.
could_not_verify: The Build Systems a la Carte paper text (the PDF was unreadable through the fetch tool); early-cutoff and trace-type definitions rest on the authors' slides and on Bazel, Salsa and rustc documentation. GHC recompilation-avoidance documentation was not read.
Mem0's re-run of Zep at 58.44% and the original GitHub issue, seen only in search summaries; no resolution of the Mem0 and Zep dispute found.

Whether MemoryAgentBench configured Zep, Mem0 and Cognee as their vendors recommend, and why they scored low; the paper does not say, and recency was encoded as serial numbers in text rather than Zep's native timestamps.

Bodies of DreamBench-SWE (stale-suppression design), KCoEvo, the two agent-memory surveys, CoCC, DocPrism, RepoAgent and DocAgent; cited from abstracts or search summaries only. VibeMemBench's last 19k characters were not read and the authors' independence from the four systems' vendors was not stated in what I read.
Any independent evaluation of Graphiti or Zep as a coding-agent memory: one search found none, and absence of results is not proof of absence.
Any controlled study that caches LLM-made conclusions about code, invalidates by dependency and measures agent tokens and success: two extended searches found only neighbours.
Star counts for graphify differed across sources (3.7k, 41.6k, 88k, 146.9k); only the README figure as fetched is reported. graphify's BENCHMARKS.md was not read.

Per-kind token numbers of the finished test's structured questions (31 against 695 tokens comes from the task description), and whether dependency recording is feasible in all three engines (specified for the in-memory reference only).

graphrag.summary: Graph-plus-summary retrieval (GraphRAG and relatives) was built for whole-corpus questions over prose. Independent benchmarks show small and inconsistent gains on ordinary QA, losses on single-fact lookup, and mostly higher query tokens and 10-1000x indexing cost. For coding agents there is no rigorous evidence for community detection plus LLM summaries; the evidence that exists concerns parser-built structural graphs (helpful for small models, modest for frontier models, tied with grep in two tiny tests). The owner is right that the finished test never covered model-extracted meaning, summaries, orientation questions, or an agent in the loop, and that the single study excluding model-extracted graphs is weak (45 questions, one author, one repo carries the whole effect, thin LLM-graph design). He is not supported on two points: star counts are adoption not effect, and Graphify (about 147k stars) builds its code graph with a deterministic tree-sitter parser, so its popularity says nothing for model-extracted code graphs. Full notes are in the notes file.

findings.claim: Graphs with summaries help on whole-corpus sensemaking, as measured by their own authors, but the judging method is biased and most of the lift comes from summarising everything rather than from the graph.
findings.evidence: GraphRAG: 72-83% win rate on comprehensiveness vs vector retrieval (podcast), 72-80% (news), 62-82% on diversity; vs map-reduce over raw text (no graph) only 'small, consistent gains' except at root level. Corpora about 1M tokens, 125 questions each. Root-level summaries used about 2.5% of the query tokens of map-reduce over raw text (not vs vector retrieval). Indexing about 281 min with gpt-4-turbo.
findings.how_measured: Authors' own benchmark; LLM judge, 5 repeats per pair; baselines vector RAG (SS) and source-text map-reduce (TS)

findings.claim: The LLM-judge protocol used in GraphRAG and LightRAG evaluations is badly biased; corrected numbers shrink or reverse the claimed gains.
findings.evidence: A method compared with itself got 90 vs 10% depending on answer order; a 25-token length difference on ~200-token answers moved win rates over 50 points. LightRAG vs plain RAG (Agriculture) fell from the reported 66.70% to 39.06% after correction; LightRAG vs MGRAG 56.38% to 32.33%. Also GPT-4o picked the first-shown summary 97-100% in some comparisons in the RAG-vs-GraphRAG study.
findings.how_measured: Independent re-evaluation with order-swapped, length-controlled judging and self-comparison sanity checks

findings.claim: On single-fact and detail questions plain retrieval ties or beats graph methods in every independent benchmark read; graphs help on multi-hop, temporal and summary-style questions, and only some graph methods do.
findings.evidence: NQ F1: plain RAG 64.78, Community-local 63.01, Community-global 54.48, triple-only KG 34.28 (Llama-3.1-8B). MultiHop-RAG accuracy: RAG 67.02, Community-local 69.01, HippoRAG2 70.27; temporal questions RAG 30.70 vs about 50 for graph methods; null questions RAG 96.01 vs Community-global 19.27. GraphRAG-Bench (Novel) fact retrieval RAG-rerank 60.92 vs MS-GraphRAG 49.29; complex reasoning 42.93 vs 50.93 (MS-GraphRAG) and 53.38 (HippoRAG2); Medical: MS-GraphRAG below plain RAG on all task types (e.g. 38.63 vs 64.73 on fact retrieval) while HippoRAG2 is at or above. Microsoft's own docs recommend Basic (vector) search where it suffices.
findings.how_measured: Independent benchmarks with one protocol across methods; accuracy/F1 per task type; Llama-3.1-8B and 70B readers (2502.11371), GPT-4o-mini (2506.05690)

findings.claim: On textbook QA, graph methods give gains under 2 points over plain keyword search and half of them are at or below it, with a no-retrieval floor only about 1 point below BM25.
findings.evidence: Average accuracy: BM-25 71.66, TF-IDF 71.71, no retrieval 70.68; RAPTOR 73.58, HippoRAG 72.64, GraphRAG 72.50, GFM-RAG 72.10, KGP 71.86, ToG 71.71, LightRAG 71.22, G-Retriever 69.84, DALK 69.30. All graph methods hurt math. Construction tokens: RAPTOR 10.1M, KG methods about 33M, GraphRAG 79.9M, LightRAG 83.9M.
findings.how_measured: Independent benchmark (16 disciplines, 20 textbooks), GPT-4o-mini, nine methods vs BM-25/TF-IDF/no-retrieval
findings.strength: strong on headline, medium on generality

findings.claim: Gains are in answer quality, not tokens: query-time tokens are mostly higher than plain retrieval, indexing is much higher, and a token-matched plain-RAG control erased most of the gain in one benchmark.
findings.evidence: Per-query tokens: vanilla RAG 879; HippoRAG2 1,008; RAPTOR 3,441; MS-GraphRAG local 38,707; LightRAG 100,832; MS-GraphRAG global 331,375. Community-GraphRAG retrieved 9,770 vs 3,631 tokens (MultiHop-RAG). Token-matched RAG scored 71.01 vs 71.17 for GraphRAG (70B reader, MultiHop-RAG). Construction time 135 s (RAG) vs 5,560 s (Community-GraphRAG). HippoRAG 2 indexing 9.2M input tokens vs 115.5M (GraphRAG) and 68.5M (LightRAG) on an 11.6k-passage corpus. Total tokens on LongBench-v2: RAG 32.9M, RAPTOR 85.9M, HippoRAG2 220.6M.
findings.how_measured: Independent token counting per query and per build; token-matched control in Appendix C of 2502.11371

findings.claim: Indexing-cost reductions exist but each is vs a specific baseline and mostly vendor-reported.
findings.evidence: LazyGraphRAG: indexing 'identical to vector RAG and 0.1% of full GraphRAG', matching global-search quality at 'more than 700 times lower query cost' (AP news, 5,590 articles, 100 synthetic queries, LLM judge; did not beat GraphRAG global at lowest budget). Dynamic community selection: 77% average token cost reduction, no significant quality difference (50 queries). HippoRAG: 10-30x cheaper than iterative retrieval (IRCoT), not than single-step retrieval. Tree structures (RAPTOR) are cheapest to build; rich KGs cost up to about 40x a tree.
findings.how_measured: Vendor blog benchmarks with LLM judges; independent cost taxonomy in 2503.04338
findings.strength: weak to medium (LazyGraphRAG, dynamic selection); strong (cost taxonomy)

findings.claim: HippoRAG 2 is the most consistent graph method: near plain-retrieval query cost with modest quality gains confirmed independently; its own gains are small versus a strong dense retriever.
findings.evidence: Own benchmark: average F1 59.8 vs 57.0 for NV-Embed-v2; recall at 5 78.2 vs 73.4; query 1.2 s vs 0.3 s; needs a 70B extraction model. HippoRAG 1: 2Wiki recall at 5 89.1 vs 68.2, but HotpotQA 77.7 vs 79.3. Independent: HippoRAG2 70.27 vs RAG 67.02 on MultiHop-RAG; 1,008 vs 879 tokens per query. The paper's LightRAG F1 of 6.6 looks like a failed reproduction.
findings.how_measured: Authors' benchmark vs dense retrievers; confirmed in two independent benchmarks

findings.claim: No rigorous study shows community detection plus LLM summaries helps a coding agent; the nearest evidence is for parser-built structural graphs as agent tools, plus a few summary-based retrieval studies.
findings.evidence: (a) Code Isn't Memory: Claude Opus 4.7, 91 tasks, tree-sitter+embeddings+call-graph index: localisation at 5 84.5% vs 44.3% same harness without vs 75.3% agentic-grep tool; resolve 50.4 vs 41.9 vs 45.3%; index vs without p=0.003, turns 28.3 vs 36.2, per-task cost $1.15 vs $1.19 (p=0.73); index vs agentic grep resolve p=0.087 and localisation p=0.080 (not significant); likely vendor-authored. (b) Small-agents study, 10 open models, SWE-bench Verified 500 tasks: graph tools Qwen3-4B 26.8 to 37.1, Qwen3-8B 16.7 to 27.4, Qwen3-32B 32.0 to 34.0 function Acc@10; gain peaks 17-21 points at 1.7-4B and shrinks to 4-5 at 32B; embeddings matched the graph at larger sizes. (c) gl-code-search: grep, grep+Graphify and grep alone all 100% (SWE-bench Lite) and 85% (fresh issues), 20 issues, extra tools rarely called. (d) File summaries: role-aware summaries up to +40% Hit@5 over bare paths, but raw source often wins; Agentless Hit@6 0.898 to 0.918. (e) Hierarchical NL summaries, one proprietary 46-repo Java system, 87 tickets: Pass@10 0.82 vs 0.57-0.62 for Cursor/Copilot/GraphCodeBERT. (f) Cursor semantic search (embeddings): +12.5% average on its own offline eval.
findings.how_measured: (a) paired Wilcoxon, within-harness ablation, n=75-80; (b) McNemar/GEE/bootstrap, no multiple-comparison correction; (c) 20 issues one model; (d)(e) retrieval Hit@k and Pass@k on benchmark/industrial data; (f) vendor offline and online A/B, no variance reported

findings.claim: The study that excluded model-extracted graphs is weak, and its LLM-graph arm was a thin design; stronger evidence either way is indirect.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2601.08773: 3 Java repos, 15 questions each, one author, Gemini (version unnamed), single annotator, no stats. Correct of 45: no-graph 31, LLM graph 38, parser graph 43. ThingsBoard no-graph already 14/15, so the gap sits in Shopizer (6/15 baseline; LLM graph 13/15; parser graph 15/15). LLM graph = class-name nodes with one generic depends_on edge, files cut to 15,000 characters, 377 Shopizer files skipped; parser graph had typed injects/extends/implements edges. Cost: $0.79 vs $0.09 (Shopizer), $6.80 vs $0.317 (two larger repos). Indirect support for parsers: 24 LLMs lose to static analysers PyCG/Jelly on call-graph generation in Python and JavaScript (models win on type inference); graph-builder quality changes prose results (GPT-4o builder 75.08 vs GPT-4o-mini 71.17 on MultiHop-RAG; only about 65% of answer entities land in the graph). No benchmark of model-extracted semantic relations (responsibility, intent) vs parser graphs exists that I could find.
findings.how_measured: Small human-labelled QA study; independent call-graph benchmark of 24 LLMs vs static tools (precision/recall not read); prose-RAG builder ablation
findings.strength: weak (excluding study); medium to strong (call-graph result); medium (builder sensitivity)

findings.claim: Graphify (about 146.9k stars) builds its code graph with a deterministic tree-sitter parser; model extraction is for docs, PDFs, images and audio; its token claim is vs reading all raw files and its README states no accuracy evaluation.
findings.evidence: README: code parsed locally with tree-sitter 'deterministic, no LLM'; edges tagged EXTRACTED/INFERRED; Leiden clustering. Worked examples: 71.5x reduction on 52 files, 5.4x on 4 files, about 1x on 6 files (httpx), baseline = reading raw files; README says savings scale with corpus size and small corpora fit in a context window. 146.9k stars and 14.1k forks are adoption, not an effect size. One fetch showed a benchmark table (LOCOMO n=300, LongMemEval-S n=50, ERPNext n=6 82.0% vs 70.8% grep) but later fetches found no benchmark file, so it is unconfirmed.
findings.how_measured: Self-reported by the tool's authors; baseline is read-everything; n tiny where given

findings.claim: Community detection itself may produce 'phantom' communities on sparse graphs; a hypothesis to test on any code graph before paying for summaries.
findings.evidence: Structureless synthetic graph: 159 leaf communities, 197 billed summaries, p=0.875; three novels: 65 of 83 billed summaries (78%) unsupported by a degree-preserving null test. Regex-extracted character networks only, repo has 0 stars and no review.
findings.how_measured: Single-author degree-preserving permutation test on synthetic and three public-domain novels

findings.claim: In the unified-framework study 'TKG' means textual knowledge graph, not temporal knowledge graph; no study of temporal graph structures for agent retrieval was found in this lane.
findings.evidence: Taxonomy in the paper: TreeKG, passage graph, KG, TKG (textual KG), RKG (rich KG). The only 'temporal' result found concerns questions with time content (MultiHop-RAG temporal: RAG 30.70 vs about 50 for graph methods), not time-stamped graph structure.
findings.how_measured: Reading of the paper's taxonomy and results tables

what_it_means_for_the_test: The owner is right that the finished test cannot speak for 'graphs' in general: it tested parser-extracted typed facts on structural and co-change questions, and did not test model-extracted meaning, summaries, community-summary retrieval, orientation questions, or an agent in the loop.

The owner's suspicion that the one excluding study was too thin is correct (45 questions, one author, one repo carries the whole effect, thin LLM-graph design), but the stronger indirect evidence (static analysers beat LLMs on call graphs; builder quality sensitivity) still leans toward parsers for syntactic relations. The open gap is semantic relations that parsers cannot produce.

Do not read Graphify's or GraphRAG's star counts as an effect size; Graphify's code graph is parser-built, so it resembles the finished test's graph plus community detection rather than contradicting it.

Highest-value additions: (1) an agent-in-the-loop arm (agentic grep alone vs grep plus the typed store as tools, scored on task success and total tokens), because only two small mixed studies address it; (2) an orientation-question arm comparing community summaries vs plain retrieval vs read-everything map-reduce, with a community-validity null test; (3) HippoRAG-2-style personalised PageRank over a model-extracted entity graph of docs and comments only, alongside the parser graph; (4) a LazyGraphRAG-style no-LLM-at-index graph for docs; (5) role-aware file summaries as an added index.

Every arm needs a no-retrieval floor and a token-matched plain-retrieval control (both changed conclusions in independent studies), and answers should be scored against ground truth or with order-swapped, length-controlled judging, not a single-order LLM judge.

Expect different outcomes by model size: structural graph tools gave 17-21 points to 1.7-4B models and only 2-5 points at 32B, and a frontier model with agentic grep was not significantly beaten by an index (p=0.08-0.09), so the agent model used in the test must be named and matched to the intended deployment.
could_not_verify: Full text of arXiv 2606.22417 (PDF undecodable; only an HTML summary was used), 2607.11046 and 2610.33958 (read only to about 100,000 characters of 124,271 and 204,116), and whether the authors of 2606.22417 sell the tool they tested.
LocAgent, RepoGraph and CodexGraph numbers beyond their abstract pages; the Code Graph Model graph-vs-no-graph ablation (truncated).
GraphRAG-Bench (Xiang) graph-construction cost appendix and the accuracy tables of the unified-framework paper 2503.04338 (truncated); CheapRAG results.

The Graphify benchmark table (LOCOMO, LongMemEval-S, ERPNext n=6): one fetch showed it, later fetches and the folder listing showed no benchmark file; also how the 71.5x token figure is computed (the README does not say).
DeepDiscovery (arXiv 2606.22906): PDF unreadable through the tool; contents unknown.
HippoRAG 2's reported LightRAG F1 of 6.6 looks like a failed reproduction; not checked.
Precision and recall figures of the 24-LLM vs static-analyser call-graph study (only the abstract page was read); the error-rate claims from other call-graph studies came from a search snippet only.
Any independent replication of LazyGraphRAG or BenchmarkQED numbers (none found; all from the same Microsoft group).
Any study of temporal knowledge graphs (time-stamped edges) as a retrieval structure for agents; none found in this lane.
The web-fetch tool returns a small model's summary of each page, so numbers are as that summary reported them and were not independently re-read from raw pages.

agents.summary: The owner is right that the finished test had no agent in the loop, but wrong that it "failed" while graphify "works". No controlled evidence was found that a graph tool raises a frontier agent's success against ordinary search tools. The best-controlled study (170,500 episodes, pre-registered, with a placebo arm, small open-weight models) found the embedding index explained the gain better than the graph. For frontier agents, the reported effect is fewer tool calls and usually fewer tokens, with success flat or slightly lower. That is the same mechanism as our 31-versus-695-token result. Graphify's headline "71.5x" is a size estimate against reading every file, with no model run. Its one agent-level code result is 82.0 % versus 70.8 % key-fact coverage on 6 questions at about 1.3x the baseline tokens. The graph it builds for code is the same kind of deterministic parser graph we used, not a temporal knowledge graph. Independent users report equal or higher token use. Star count is adoption only.

findings.claim: Pre-registered, placebo-controlled study: the embedding index, not the code-graph tools, carries the localisation gain in small agents; graph tools on top of embeddings add little.
findings.evidence: 9 open-weight models, 170,500 episodes on 500 SWE-bench tasks, 5 seeds. Function Acc@10: Qwen3-4B grep 0.114, embedding 0.218, graph tools 0.191, both 0.214; Qwen3-14B 0.282/0.318/0.309/0.354; Qwen3-32B 0.289/0.321/0.306/0.314. 'Embedding arm is never below the graph arm.' Graph tools added to embeddings gained significantly for one model (Qwen3-14B +0.036). At 32B the tools gain is +0.026 (adjusted p=0.056). Random-entity placebo lowered accuracy for the two smallest models (-0.020, -0.044). Tokens for Qwen3-4B: 3.8k grep-only vs 3.5k with tools; steps 15.1 vs 8.4.
findings.how_measured: Authors' pre-registered design, grep-only vs graph tools vs embedding vs both vs placebo, function-level localisation Acc@10, Holm-corrected tests. Small models only, Python only. I could not confirm the author's independence from any tool and did not read the last 11k characters or the hop-stratified results.

findings.claim: Graphify's '71.5x fewer tokens per query' is a size ratio, not an agent measurement.
findings.evidence: About 123k estimated corpus tokens divided by about 1.7k average graph-answer tokens for 5 fixed questions on a 52-file self-curated corpus (3 repos, 5 papers, 4 diagrams). No model call, no answer-correctness check; baseline is reading all raw files, which the project's own analysis calls the worst possible strategy. Its 6-file example is about 1x and the page says small corpora gain little. Extraction cost is excluded. Independent analyses found no reproduction harness or fixtures.
findings.how_measured: Word count to tokens (100 words to 133 tokens), answer characters / 4, ratio of the two; run inline by the tool.

findings.claim: Graphify's only agent-in-the-loop code result is small, self-run, and costs more tokens than the baseline.
findings.evidence: ERPNext (about 1M lines Python), fixed agent (Claude Opus 4.8), up to 14 turns, n=6 questions, key-fact coverage 82.0 % with graphify versus 70.8 % grep/read baseline, about 140k tokens per query. A secondary write-up states graphify used about 1.3x baseline tokens, cost about $0.320 vs $0.322, and other retrieval tools scored 79.1-80.5 %. The benchmark page gives no per-arm token or turn counts. Its LOCOMO results are conversational memory, not code; there graph-expand 45.3 % vs seed-only 42.7 % at n=300 (one standard error about 2.9 points by my arithmetic) is inside noise. Its temporal ERPNext suite (689 weekly checkpoints) has no QA results.
findings.how_measured: Maintainers' own harness, judge validated at 90.6 % agreement with a second judge on a sample; no independent party. The 1.3x token and 79-80 % figures are from a secondary page, not the primary.

findings.claim: Independent users of graphify and a similar tool report equal or higher token or dollar cost, and mixed quality.
findings.evidence: GitHub issue 985: one user, 1,484 files, each query about 2k tokens, grep workflows often cheaper; another, Copilot CLI on a .NET monorepo, graphify MCP cost about 1.6-1.9x a code-only agent with higher peak context and partial answers. CodeGraph replication on Hono (Opus 4.8, 5 questions x 4 repeats x 2 arms): tool calls 14.0 to 6.3, tokens 9,385 to 7,261 (-22.6 %), cost $0.338 to $0.361 (+6.8 %); answers identical; the tool's README claims -71 % calls and -35 % cost. First run silently never connected the tool.
findings.how_measured: User-reported A/B in issue comments (anecdote); a single-author replication with 40 valid runs and per-run connection checks; one single-lookup test (628 vs 13,659 tokens) explicitly not a session.

findings.claim: With a frontier agent, map-based code tools cut tokens 17-39 % mainly by displacing file reads, with success about flat and test-generation tokens up.
findings.evidence: Claude Code, Haiku 4.5 low effort, built-ins pinned. LinuxFLBench n=152: recall@10 0.717 to 0.757-0.829, tokens 1,008,163 to 610,910-754,768. SWE-bench Pro n=253: resolved 49.0 % vs 44.3-50.6 % (inside about 3-point noise), tokens 3,116,193 to 2,310,653-2,590,046. SWT-bench n=161: tokens and time up. SecBench n=166: callgraph 34.3 % vs 28.9 %. Tool calls 25.4 to 8.5-13.1 (LinuxFLBench), 44.5 to 3.4-5.2 (Pro). Fewer-token runs are read-displacement cases (109/109 for callgraph on LinuxFLBench). A BM25-only docs arm ties the call graph on LinuxFLBench (0.770). A hook forces one map query before reads, so steering and graph are confounded.
findings.how_measured: Authors' controlled arms, one run per task, no significance tests; map-construction cost excluded; token definition not clear in what I read.

findings.claim: Graph tools are often not used unless steered, and can lose to BM25 on some task types.
findings.evidence: CodeCompass, Claude Sonnet 4.5, 258 trials on a 3,500-line FastAPI repo: 51 of 88 graph-condition trials (58 %) made no graph call despite instruction; those scored 80.2 % coverage vs 99.5 % for the 37 that used it. Coverage by group (vanilla / BM25 / graph): semantic 90.0/100.0/88.9; structural 79.7/85.1/76.4; hidden-dependency 76.2/78.2/99.4. Prompt was changed for the hidden group only. No token data. Hono replication: on a control question the tool was never invoked.
findings.how_measured: Single-author preprint; metric is fraction of required files read or edited, not working code; paper has internal inconsistencies (42/38/61 % adoption, 20 vs 23.2 point gain).

findings.claim: Codebase-Memory: about 10x fewer tokens per question but 9 points lower answer quality than a file-reading agent.
findings.evidence: Tree-sitter property graph in SQLite, 14 MCP tools, 31 repos (one per language); 83 % vs 92 % answer quality; about 10x fewer tokens and 2.1x fewer tool calls (earlier notes: about 1,000 vs 10,000 tokens per question, 2.3 vs 4.8 calls, Opus 4.6 both arms). Graph arm won hub detection and caller ranking on 19 of 31 languages; explorer won full-source and exhaustive-grep questions.
findings.how_measured: Preprint by the tool's authors; first author grades per earlier notes; question counts small; indexing cost excluded.

findings.claim: Research localisation systems (RepoGraph, LocAgent, CodexGraph, KGCompass, CGM) report gains on SWE-bench Lite, but token cost rises or is not reported, ablations are inside each author's own system, and nothing is independently replicated.
findings.evidence: RepoGraph: resolved +2-2.3 points on three agents, tokens up in every case (Agentless 42,376 to 47,323); 2-hop flattened 26.00 % is below the 27.33 % baseline at 10,505 graph tokens. LocAgent: file-level up to 92.7 %, 32B fine-tuned about 86 % cheaper; ablation (earlier notes) removing SearchEntity costs 19 points file Acc@5 vs about 2 for removing TraverseGraph. CodexGraph: 102.25k tokens vs AutoCodeRover 76.01k, equal 22.96 % on Lite, collapses on a weaker model (1.95 % vs 9.34 %). KGCompass (graph of issues, PRs, files, classes, functions): 58.3 % Lite, 56.0 % function localisation, about $0.20 per repair, abstract only, earlier notes record 15.3 % in another harness. CGM: 43.00 % Lite via a trained model.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14684 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09089 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03910 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21710 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16901 ; research/lane-agent-graphs.txt
findings.how_measured: Authors' own papers on SWE-bench Lite or similar, mostly one run, Python only; abstracts re-checked this session, tables from earlier notes.

findings.claim: Where savings exist they come from fewer reads and fewer tool calls, smaller capped outputs, and steering; non-graph methods save as much.
findings.evidence: FlowPlan (planning, no graph): tokens 0.32x-0.76x of baseline on SWE-bench Verified/Pro with Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5, resolved rates not significantly different (McNemar). FastContext explorer subagent: 457k to 338k tokens (-26 %) with 71.7 to 74.7 resolved on SWE-bench Multilingual (GPT-5.4). Augment (vendor, harness differs): -30 % tokens, -23 % cost, 61.8 vs 59.9 % on SWE-Bench Pro, attributed to fewer cache reads. Cursor A/B with same model: code retention +0.3 % overall, +2.6 % in 1,000+ file repos, grep plus semantic search best. Cognition: over 60 % of first turn spent retrieving context; precision favoured because polluted context hurt more than missing context. Claude Code's builder says they moved from a vector index to glob/grep (index drifts, security, 'outperformed by a lot' on partly internal 'vibes' comparisons), at a cost in latency and tokens, no numbers. AGENTS.md study (abstract): overview files raised cost over 20 % without a general success gain.
findings.how_measured: Authors or vendors on their own benchmarks; Cursor includes a live A/B on real traffic; FlowPlan has McNemar tests; Augment and Cognition are vendor posts (Augment seen via search summary).

findings.claim: Reading and searching are a large but variable share of agent tokens in published traces; most counted tokens are re-read cache reads.
findings.evidence: SWE-Pruner: read 76.1 %, execute 12.1 %, edit 11.8 % (Mini SWE Agent, Sonnet 4.5; GLM-4.6 read 67.5 %). FastContext: reading and searching 56.2 % of tool-use turns and 46.5 % of main-agent tokens (GPT-5.4, 300 SWE-bench Multilingual trajectories). FlowPlan: about two-thirds of tokens after the first edit; cache reads 96-98 % of tokens. Token study (8 models, 500 problems, OpenHands): cache reads dominate volume and cost, input spikes from file views and test output, same-task runs differ by up to 30x (abstract) vs about 2x (body). SHERLOC (summary only): reasoning 19.5k vs tool output 9.0k tokens for Qwen3-235B thinking. The owner's 27 % fetched content and 59 % orchestrator window are a different agent shape (long multi-turn orchestrator) from these short SWE-bench episodes.
findings.how_measured: Authors' trajectory analyses with different agents, models and token definitions (cumulative vs unique not stated in SWE-Pruner and FastContext); not comparable with each other.

findings.claim: What graphify builds is a deterministic code property graph plus LLM-extracted document concepts; it is not a temporal knowledge graph, and no source shows temporal graphs helping coding agents.
findings.evidence: Graphify code: tree-sitter AST, about 40 languages, no LLM, edges tagged EXTRACTED or INFERRED (calls, imports, inherits, mixes_in), Leiden communities, query depth 2 and 2,000-token budget, hooks nudging Claude Code and Gemini CLI toward the graph; docs, PDFs, images go through an LLM pass. Its temporal part is weekly AST checkpoints with no QA results. Git2KG mines temporal graphs from git for socio-technical analysis; GREPO uses temporal anchors for graph neural network localisation; AgenticSZZ targets bug-inducing commits; Axon adds co-change edges with no evaluation. Graphiti/Zep is a temporal graph for conversation memory with self-reported scores and no independent reproduction found.
findings.how_measured: Readme and benchmark page reading for graphify; search-summary-level reading for the temporal systems (no evaluations of the kind the owner asks about were found).
findings.strength: medium for what graphify is; no evidence on temporal graphs for agents

findings.claim: Recurring design choices in tools that report gains: deterministic parsers, a lexical entry point before traversal, 1-2 hop capped expansion, token-capped outputs of paths and signatures, a few on-demand tools beside grep and read, steering so the tool gets used, incremental updates, and lightweight stores.
findings.evidence: Parser vs LLM graph (Java, 3 repos): 15/15 correct at $0.09 and 22 s vs 13/15 at $0.79 and 215 s (earlier notes, weak to medium). LocAgent ablation: lexical search tool matters far more than traversal. RepoGraph: 2-hop uncapped hurt. Aider 1k-token map budget, graphify 2,000-token query budget. Codebase-Memory about 1.2 s incremental re-index; SQLite or NetworkX in the working systems; the only graph database in the agent studies (Neo4j in CodexGraph) ran out of memory on 43 tasks and used the most tokens. No source holds facts and algorithm fixed while varying the engine, so our identical answers across three engines is unpublished elsewhere.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08773 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09089 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14684 ; https://aider.chat/docs/repomap.html ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03910 ; research/lane-agent-graphs.txt
findings.how_measured: Synthesis across the sources above; most items are design observations from tools and papers rather than isolated ablations.

what_it_means_for_the_test: The next test needs an agent in the loop with model and harness held fixed, measuring per task: cumulative tokens and uncached tokens separately, turns, tool calls, success against a checked answer, and wall time, plus build and tool-description tokens. This is where the owner is right.

Arms should include grep-and-read only, a lexical/BM25 symbol search with the same capped output format, an embedding search, the typed graph tool, graph plus lexical, and a placebo returning plausible but wrong entities. The placebo and the lexical/embedding arm are the controls missing from almost every code-graph paper except the one pre-registered study.

Check in every run that the tool server connected and the tool was actually called; two independent sources lost whole runs to silent non-connection, and one paper found 58 % of graph-condition trials made no graph call.
Test steering (a hook or short orientation file) as its own condition so graph effect and steering effect are separable; the published positive results confound them.

Report by task type (cross-file navigation, impact analysis, edit, test writing) and repeat each condition several times; treat differences under 3 to 5 points as noise at 100 to 300 tasks. Expect no gain or a loss on edit and test-writing tasks.

Keep the graph deterministic and add natural-language nodes (docs, commit messages, issues) and a temporal layer as separately switchable arms, so the owner's question about knowledge graphs versus temporal knowledge graphs becomes a measured contrast. No source gives evidence either way for the temporal layer in coding agents.

Do not treat graphify's 71.5x or its 82.0 vs 70.8 % as an effect size to match: one is a size ratio against reading everything, the other is n=6 at about 1.3x tokens. Our 31 vs about 695 token result on questions is the same mechanism the tools report; the open question is whether it survives inside an agent and what it does to success.
Non-graph levers (explorer subagent, planning, capped lexical search output) saved as many or more tokens in published tests, so they should be arms beside the graph rather than assumed away.

Compare token shares carefully: published read shares of 46 % to 76 % come from short single-task episodes; the owner's 27 % fetched content and 59 % orchestrator window come from a long multi-turn orchestrator where re-sent context dominates, and most counted tokens in published traces (96-98 % in one) are cache re-reads.
could_not_verify: Graphify's BENCHMARKS.md gives no per-arm token or turn counts; the 1.3x tokens, $0.320 vs $0.322 cost, and 79.1-80.5 % scores for other tools come from a secondary write-up, not the primary page.
Why graphify's stars roughly doubled (about 69k in June to 146.9k as read now); no history series obtained.

Serena: documentation describes self-graded agent runs with no token or call totals in the pages I read; no independent measurement found. No agent-level measurement of language-server or SCIP tools found.

GitNexus 68.4 % vs 37.0 % (a directory site citing a vendor report I could not locate) and code-review-graph per-repo ratios (6.8x to 82x): primary reports and reproduction not opened; treated as unverified.
The Orbit graph token-usage benchmark pages returned 404; a search summary of an accuracy comparison for a different tool was not used.
Token definitions (cumulative processed vs unique) in 2611.07286, SWE-Pruner and FastContext were not clear in what the fetch tool returned.
arXiv 2608.13867 (Engineering Reliable Coding Agents): only the contents and abstract reached me, so its evidence on when to keep a typed index is unread.
KGCompass: abstract only, no independent reproduction, repair model behind 58.3 % unnamed.

Small-model study 2610.33958: last 11k characters and the hop-stratified results not read; an earlier version's hop figures (odds multiplied by 0.47-0.55 per extra hop) are from a superseded version; author independence from any tool not established.
Augment and SHERLOC figures are from search summaries, not the primary pages.
No decomposition exists in the sources I found of how much of a graph tool's token saving is the avoided read versus the avoided later re-reads of that read.
Nothing was run or installed; all fetched pages are small-model extractions, not raw text.

evaluation.summary: The finished test scored co-change and ran no agent, so it cannot answer the owner's question about tokens, turns or mistakes. The owner is right on that. He is not shown right that "graphs fail", and the finished test's own addendum 6 forbids that wording. The graphify headline the owner points to is a size ratio: whole-corpus tokens divided by graph-answer tokens, with no model called and no answers graded. Its README reports accuracy only on conversation-memory sets and a code-like set of n = 6, both self-reported. I found no independent, controlled, paired agent study of a code knowledge graph. The two closest studies are by the tools' own authors, with weak design details. I propose five designs: a replayed-commit live agent ablation (D1), an execution-derived break oracle (D2), recorded-session lookup replay for screening only (D3), a cached-conclusion invalidation test over replayed history (D4), and a fresh typed-question set with an agent in the loop (D5). A realistic main run is about 40 tasks x 3 arms x 3 runs after a 12-task pilot. That detects roughly a 12 to 16 percent token change; a +10 point success change is out of reach on this repo. All sizing figures are my own calculation, not source figures.

findings.claim: Graphify's published benchmark measures size, not quality: whole-corpus token estimate divided by average graph-answer size over five fixed questions; no model call, no grading.
findings.evidence: Docs page: corpus tokens estimated from word count (about 133 tokens per 100 words); each answer is up to 3 matched nodes with a 3-hop breadth-first search written as text; authors say it does not check correctness, speed or cost and that small repos (under about 50,000 words) may not benefit. The 71.5x figure in secondary articles (52-file mixed corpus, about 1,700 versus 123,000 tokens) is this ratio, per a search summary.
findings.how_measured: Read the vendor's own documentation page; no independent run.
findings.strength: weak for any claim about agents (honest about itself)

findings.claim: Graphify's README accuracy benchmarks are on conversation-memory sets plus one code-like set of 6 questions, all self-reported; stars are adoption, not effect.
findings.evidence: LOCOMO n=300: recall@10 0.497 but QA accuracy 45.3% versus supermemory 49.7%; LongMemEval-S n=50: 76%, tied with dense RAG; ERPNext cross-tool n=6: key-fact coverage 82.0% versus grep-and-read baseline 70.8%. Judge validated against a second judge (90.6% agreement, kappa 0.81). Header showed about 147k stars (another source said 88k at a different date).
findings.source: https://github.com/safishamsi/graphify (via page summary); BENCHMARKS.md returned 404 at two URLs
findings.how_measured: Authors' own harness; run counts, who ran it and ERPNext design not verifiable.

findings.claim: The best controlled graph-versus-no-graph agent design found is an on/off ablation with 3 seeds, but it is by the tool's own authors and underpowered on success.
findings.evidence: 91 instances (SWE-PolyBench Verified and SWE-bench Pro), Claude Opus 4.7, same harness with index tools on versus off, 3 seeds, git scrub plus post-run leak audit (26 cells excluded). Localisation acc@5 44.3 to 84.5%; resolve 41.9 to 50.4% (p=0.003); cost per run unchanged (p=0.73). Versus a grep harness: resolve 50.4 vs 45.3% (p=0.087, not significant). Wilcoxon, unadjusted, no intervals; authors flag conflict of interest.
findings.how_measured: Vendor's own harness, paired by instance, mean of 3 seeds.

findings.claim: Codebase-Memory's graph agent used about one tenth of the tokens but scored lower quality than file exploration, graded by the tool's author with no run counts or intervals.
findings.evidence: 31 repos (one per language), 12 fixed questions, Claude Opus 4.6 both arms: quality 0.83 vs 0.92, tokens about 1,000 vs about 10,000 per question, tool calls 2.3 vs 4.8. Explorer better on full source context (16 of 31) and exhaustive call-site grep (10 of 31). Explorer's tool set and budget not described.
findings.how_measured: First author graded against references from manual inspection; no judge, no inter-rater check.

findings.claim: Needed-but-unchanged context has working label recipes: execution-based (apply production diff without test edits), change-evidence rules (code2test, edit2ripple, trace2code, comment2context), expert annotation with a sufficiency test, and follow-on-reasoning rules for mined session reads. Logged agent reads miss all gold files on 27 to 35% of samples, so reads alone are a poor label.
findings.evidence: TEBench builds parent / non-test-changes-applied / full-commit versions (314 tasks after filtering 67,670 commits). Agent Retrieval Bench: 427 samples, logged trajectories miss all gold on 35.2% (OpenAI) and 27.2 to 29.3% (Codex). ContextBench: 1,136 tasks, gold checked by whether GPT-5 given only that context passes the tests; no formal rule for needed-but-not-edited.
findings.how_measured: Benchmark papers; mostly single-run, descriptive, no intervals.

findings.claim: Agent token use is noisy: within one cell the median geometric SD is x1.34 on one model and five tasks; spread scales with mean cost; single-run pass@1 varies 2.2 to 6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified.
findings.evidence: 2,700 runs (5 tasks x 12 specs x 3 effort levels x 15 repeats), per-spec medians x1.29 to x1.40, log-log slope 1.08. Separate study: 4 runs per problem, 8 models, most expensive run about 2x the cheapest on average and up to 30x in some cases (not reconciled in the page). 10 runs per task on 500 tasks: single-run SD 0.7 to 1.8 points; +2 points at SD 1.5 needs 9 runs, +1 point needs 36.
findings.how_measured: Repeated runs of agents on SWE-bench Verified tasks; token variance studies by independent authors, pass@1 study with 60,000 trajectories.

findings.claim: Future-history and online leaks are real in agent evaluations; the controls are single-commit repo, no network, blind transcript audit, and non-public repos.
findings.evidence: SWE-bench issue 465: agents used git log --all, remote branches, reflog, tags, dangling objects to find the fix; fixed in v4.1.0. Cursor audit of 731 trajectories: 63% of successful runs retrieved the fix (57% online, 9% from bundled .git); sealing history and limiting internet dropped scores from 87.1 to 73.0% and 74.7 to 54.0% for two models. The finished test mounted the live working tree (full history) read-only in every arm container (addendum 6 item 7).
findings.how_measured: Maintainers' tracker; vendor blind auditor over 731 trajectories.

findings.claim: No benchmark found that injects a code change and scores whether a cached conclusion about the code went stale; adjacent benchmarks are non-code (STALE, MemoryAgentBench) or small and fabricated (stale-context-bench).
findings.evidence: STALE: 400 scenarios, 1,200 queries, best model 55.2%. MemoryAgentBench: multi-hop conflict resolution at most 7% (secondary). Meetless harness: 6 and 20 fabricated facts, keyword graders, authors call rankings directional only.
findings.how_measured: Abstract / README reads; MemoryAgentBench via summaries.
findings.strength: medium-weak; gap confirmed by one search only

findings.claim: Impact-analysis ground truth from execution (inject a change, take what fails) exists in the literature and is independent of any graph extractor.
findings.evidence: Musco et al.: 10 Java projects, about 17,000 mutants; more sophisticated call graphs raised recall, the basic call graph gave the best precision-recall trade-off. A snippet said tests detect only 47% of direct and 35% of indirect artificial faults (unverified).
findings.how_measured: Mutation-based impact sets on Java programs.

findings.claim: The sample-size result for a 20% token change: about 24 tasks at 3 runs per arm if the task-by-arm spread tau is 0.30, about 13 if 0.15; roughly 52 if run-to-run SD is double; success at +10 points needs 80 to 120 tasks at 3 runs.
findings.evidence: Formula: variance of per-task mean log ratio = 2 sigma^2/k + tau^2 with sigma = ln 1.34; 80% power, two-sided 5%. n=40, k=3: min detectable token reduction 11.7% (tau 0.15) or 15.6% (tau 0.30). Success simulation: power 0.32 to 0.39 at n=30, k=3; 0.66 to 0.80 at n=80; 0.84 to 0.94 at n=120. Paired success-difference SE about 5 to 6 points at n=40, k=3.
findings.source: scratchpad/eval/power.js and se.js (my arithmetic); sigma from arXiv 2608.25399
findings.how_measured: My own calculation and simulation with assumptions written out; not a measurement of this repo; tau unknown until a pilot.

what_it_means_for_the_test: Next test must run an agent. The finished test cannot say anything about tokens, turns, success or mistakes, and its label (files the commit changed) gives zero credit to context that is read but not edited. Do not describe it as 'graphs fail'; describe it as 'stores and one ranking tweak scored on co-change'.

Add labels for needed-but-unchanged context, each kept as its own column: tests that fail when the production diff is applied without test edits, follow-on-reasoning reads from recorded sessions, files edited by a follow-up fix to the same area, invariants whose anchors the diff touches, and a sufficiency check. Build them by execution or blind reading, not from the extractor the arms share.

Run paired live arms: default tools, plus a typed store, plus a model-built graph, plus a placebo tool of equal description size. Count tool schema tokens against each arm and report uncached input, cache write, cache read and output separately. Primary outcome is tokens to a passing change, with success as a non-inferiority guard.

Size it from a pilot: 12 tasks x 4 arms x 3 runs to estimate run noise and the task-by-arm spread, then about 40 tasks x 3 arms x 3 runs. Expect to detect roughly a 12 to 16 percent token change, not a small success change.

Leak control for the model-built graph: build from a git archive of each parent, or build once at the oldest parent and update commit by commit; no .git, no network, no mounted live tree, memory files off, blind transcript audit, exclusion ledger. The finished test mounted the live tree with full history in every arm container.

Test caching and invalidation separately (D4): replay 10 to 20 commits, ask the same 40 claim-questions, compare no cache, no invalidation, time-to-live, file-hash anchored, and dependency-propagated invalidation. Only claims whose answer changed while their own anchors did not can show value from a graph; count them first.

Use fresh data. The 75 held-out commits are spent for T1 and were seen in aggregate; use them as development material for the new label kinds and take the final set from commits after the freeze or from a prospective set with a hashed protocol; report the two separately.
could_not_verify: graphify BENCHMARKS.md (404 at two URLs): ERPNext n=6 design, run counts, who ran it, and how 71.5x is defined in the repo are unverified; 71.5x corpus figures come from secondary summaries; star count differs by source (about 147k on the repo page header relayed by a summary, 88k elsewhere).

Unreadable or truncated: PDF bodies of arXiv 2608.25399 and 2604.22750 (HTML used); ContextBench appendix H (usage drop and redundancy definitions) and the last 27,705 characters of its page; the last about 25,000 characters of the Agent Retrieval Bench page.

Seen only in search summaries, not opened: RepoQA, CoReQA, CodeRepoQA, CATM/CodeGrep, MemoryAgentBench paper, SWE-Bench-CL, AgingBench, HybridRAG-Bench, 'Don't ask the LLM to track freshness', code-judge bias studies, Anthropic's 'Demystifying evals' post, the 47%/35% fault-detection claim, and the knowledge-graph build-variance snippets (94 vs 91 entities; 68% correct tuples).
No independent, controlled, paired agent study of a code knowledge graph reporting tokens, success and uncertainty was found; one may exist beyond what a few searches reached.

Unknown for this repo and needing a feasibility step: whether tests, mypy, tsc and import-linter run at old parents; how many needed-but-unchanged labels exist per commit; how many dependency-case staleness events history holds; the task-by-arm spread tau; the orientation share of an agent's tokens.

All sample-size and power figures are my own calculation or simulation with stated assumptions; the token variance input (geometric SD 1.34) comes from one model and five tasks and may understate this repo's variance.

audit.verdict:
The owner is right that the test was narrow, and the narrowing happened before any arm was built. He asked about meaning stored as relations, time and caching with invalidation, and fetching small pieces fast. The protocol turned that into one task: recall of the files a commit changed, inside a fixed 8,000-token answer, with no agent in the loop, from deterministic parser facts at one snapshot per commit. Its headline axis was the storage engine, and the answer on that axis was predicted to be exactly zero before the held-out run (addendum 3 item 21, addendum 4 item 22). Five pre-run warnings in critic.txt and verify.txt were not acted on: an agent pilot, labels for context a change needed but did not edit, an embedding arm, community summaries, and scoring the store as an addition to grep.

He is not right on three points.
1. "Experiments all failing" is false. The typed graph store beat scripted search and both floors on T1: +0.076 recall against search, interval [+0.036, +0.118]. The win is confined to mobile-app seeds; outside them it is +0.024 against search, interval [-0.024, +0.074].
2. Graphify's results are mostly not evidence of effect. The 71.5x headline is a size ratio against reading the whole corpus, with no correctness check; on code alone it is 8.8x, and it was never re-run. 146,932 stars measure adoption. Independent controlled runs on code with a strong model are null or negative. The one independent positive (graphify-bench) is on doc-and-code questions: Sonnet 5 scored 80 % with graphify against 70 % without it, and that comes from the model-read document layer our test left out.
3. Graph type is not the deciding variable. Graphify is not a temporal knowledge graph, and its code layer is the same parser-built typed graph family as ours. No source found shows that choosing graph, knowledge graph or temporal knowledge graph separates a win from a loss. What does separate them: the entry point, the output cap and format, steering, model size and task type.

assumptions.assumption: 'Graph against relational' is a contest of storage engines
assumptions.where: brief.md (owner's fairness objection); protocol.md §1 and §5; protocol-addendum-3.md E13-E14 (H1 and H2 as the primary comparison)
assumptions.status: weakly supported as a reading of the owner's objection; contradicted as a test of his question
