assumptions.why: With the same facts and the same algorithm, every engine returns the same answer (protocol §1; verify.txt verify-schema-scoring error 9). No coding-agent paper varies the engine (research/lane-agent-graphs.txt line 85). The owner asked what is stored and how it is used, not which engine stores it.
assumptions.consequence: H1 and H2 are zero by construction. SQLite held the same property graph, so all three typed arms were graph arms. The only informative contrast in the test was typed graph (any engine) against scripted search.
assumptions.fix: Keep the engine only for H5 (speed, size, update cost, effort). Vary the representation instead: parser facts, model-extracted facts, a document layer, stored conclusions, stored time validity.

assumptions.assumption: Identical answers from three engines say something about graphs
assumptions.status: contradicted as evidence about graphs; supported as an implementation check
assumptions.why: Identity follows from shared facts plus a cross-check arm. Even so, the answers shown match on 770 of 770 tasks, but the full ranked lists differ on 5 SQLite and 3 DuckPGQ tasks (refute:discipline). The only graph-native step tested was a stored Louvain community prior on personalised PageRank, and the PageRank iterations ran in application code.
assumptions.consequence: H1b: +0.015 recall, interval [-0.010, +0.042]; draws range +0.009 to +0.032; T2 -0.037. This speaks to one prior on one repository, not to graph algorithms in general.
assumptions.fix: Report identity as an implementation check only. Test the algorithms that have no cheap SQL form: multi-seed personalised PageRank, Steiner subgraphs, typed explanation paths that are scored, community summaries. Score them on tasks with several seeds and on 'explain why' tasks.

assumptions.assumption: Co-change (other files changed in the same commit) is the right primary reference
assumptions.where: protocol.md §4 T1 and §7; research/lane-scoring.txt; warned in critic.txt FAIRNESS 'Truth circularity' and in verify.txt (verify-schema-scoring error 7; the [protocol] line)
assumptions.status: weakly supported as a proxy; warned before the run and not acted on
assumptions.why: The label is the co-change signal itself. Context that is needed but not edited (callers, contracts, tests) earns zero. Before the run only 62 % of targets had ever co-changed with the seed (verify.txt).
assumptions.consequence: Half of the typed arm's credited recall (0.337 of 0.670 per task) came through paths containing a co-change edge. Outside mobile seeds the typed store ties the co-change floor: +0.001, interval [-0.051, +0.055]. The owner's 'connections that will or won't break' were never scored.
assumptions.fix: Use labels that do not come from the shared extractor, each in its own column: tests that fail when the production diff is applied without test edits; invariants whose anchors the diff touches; files touched by a follow-up fix; a blind sufficiency check (widen/lane-evaluation.md D2).

assumptions.where: research/lane-agent-graphs.txt BUILD RECS ('Do NOT use: ... LLM-extracted graphs'); HARNESS-BOTTLENECKS-2026-11.md §6 'Do not build'; protocol.md §3 (one deterministic extractor)
assumptions.status: weakly supported for syntactic relations; untested for semantic relations
assumptions.why: The direct study (arXiv 2601.08773) is weak: 45 questions, one author, a thin model-built graph, one repository carrying the effect. Parsers beating models on call graphs (arXiv 2410.00603) says nothing about intent, rationale or doc-to-code claims. The only independent positive for graphify is in its model-read document layer (graphify-bench, Sonnet 5, doc-and-code tasks: 80 % against 70 %, cost -0.084 USD, interval [-0.180, -0.005]; contradiction hunt 4 of 4 found against 2 of 4; Haiku 4.5: 75 % against 80 %).
assumptions.consequence: The test cannot speak to the layer graphify adds. This repo has much documentation: 87 markdown files, about 574k tokens (bytes/4); 517 of 1,268 backticked file names in docs do not resolve.
assumptions.fix: Add a switchable model-extracted layer over docs and comments: concepts, rationale, doc-to-code links, each with confidence and source line. Count its build tokens. Score it on doc-versus-code questions and planted contradictions with an agent in the loop. Keep code relations from the parser.

assumptions.assumption: No summaries, reports or orientation layer are needed
assumptions.where: protocol.md §3 (no summary node); critic.txt MISSING algorithms bullet (community summaries), not acted on
assumptions.status: untested here; outside evidence leans against summaries as a substitute for code and is unknown for summaries used as pointers
assumptions.why: Code summaries answered 4 of 45 behavioural questions against 27 of 45 for source (arXiv 2607.09691, abstract only). Model-written context files cost about 20 % more with no success gain (ETH AGENTS.md study). RepoGraph's 2-hop summary held resolution (28.67 % at 1,229 tokens) where the flattened 2-hop dump hurt it (26.00 % at 10,505 tokens). Across windows, 294 paths read in five or more windows hold 73 % of fetched tokens (HARNESS §6).
assumptions.consequence: Orientation questions, where graphify's report and the owner's 'small small' fetch would act, were never asked.
assumptions.fix: Add an orientation-question set. Compare community summaries, role-aware file summaries used as an index (pointer, not substitute), plain retrieval and map-reduce reading. Run a degree-preserving null test that the communities are real before paying for summaries.

assumptions.assumption: Temporal validity, caching and invalidation can be left out
assumptions.where: protocol.md §3 (one snapshot per parent; the cache is a build cache keyed by SHA); HARNESS-BOTTLENECKS-2026-11.md §6 ('Do not build ... time-based expiry'; 'a cache over traversal has nothing to save')
assumptions.status: untested; it is exactly what the owner asked about
assumptions.why: Parser facts cost zero model tokens and rebuild in about 5.3 s per commit (build-b/facts-NOTES.md), so the test had nothing expensive to cache. The primitive that could save tokens is a conclusion that carries its dependencies and is invalidated by early cutoff, as in build systems; this is strong as engineering description with no token evidence. Published temporal-graph numbers are conversation-memory results, mostly vendor-run. Independent MemoryAgentBench ranked Zep lowest: 7 % single-hop, 3 % multi-hop.
assumptions.consequence: 'Caching does not help' holds only for traversal over cheap facts. Caching conclusions that cost tokens to derive, with dependency-based invalidation, has never been tested.
assumptions.fix: Test 1: replay the 190 per-commit snapshots, record each answer's dependency set, and compare cache policies (none, whole-repo, file-hash, fact-level, fact-level with early cutoff). Test 2: report stale-served rate (must be 0), avoidable recompute and hit rate, priced with measured lookup costs. Only then an agent pilot with a no-invalidation stale control. Close a doc citation edge when its target file disappears.

assumptions.assumption: A retrieval proxy can stand in for an agent
assumptions.where: protocol.md §8 (agent pilot left to the owner); critic.txt MISSING 'An end-to-end agent evaluation' (24 to 30 commits, four tool sets), not acted on; protocol-addendum-6.md D19; no record in graph2/ that the decision was put to the owner
assumptions.status: untested; outside evidence says the proxy misses the main effect
assumptions.why: Behaviour dominates. In CodeCompass, 58 % of graph-condition trials made no graph call. Agents re-read files after a graph answer. In graphify-bench, Sonnet 5 on code used +32k tokens, interval [-8k, +75k], with accuracy 78 % against 84 %. Graph tools give +17 to 21 points at 1.7 to 4B model size and 2 to 5 at 32B.
assumptions.consequence: No claim can be made about tokens, turns, success or mistakes. This is the largest gap against the owner's actual goal.
assumptions.fix: Run agent arms with the deployment model fixed: grep only; plus BM25; plus embeddings; plus the graph tool; plus graph and lexical; plus a placebo tool of equal description size. Count tokens including subagents, uncached tokens separately, and tool-schema tokens. Check every run that the tool connected and was called. Make steering its own condition. Pilot 12 tasks x 4 arms x 3 runs, then about 40 x 3 x 3.

assumptions.assumption: A scripted search is a fair baseline
assumptions.why: About half of search's credited recall is co-change padding, and it does not beat the co-change floor: -0.013, interval [-0.032, +0.006] (refute:claims). It is not an agent searching. The embedding arm was left out although verify.txt called embeddings the strongest non-graph baseline. critic.txt asked that the stores be scored 'as additions to grep'; they were scored instead of it.
assumptions.consequence: The T1 win is over a weak, padded baseline and comes from mobile seeds. It does not show a win over how agents search today.
assumptions.fix: Use live agentic grep as the baseline. Add a BM25 symbol-search arm with the same output cap, and an embedding arm (needs a model download, the owner's decision). Score the graph as an addition to grep.

assumptions.assumption: A fixed 8,000-token answer budget measures token efficiency
assumptions.where: protocol.md §7; protocol-addendum-2.md A3; protocol-addendum-4.md item 2; grade:heldout limits bullet 1
assumptions.why: The median answer size was 7,999 tokens for every arm and set, so the tokens condition never decided a verdict. Tokens to 80 % recall, where reached: typed 7,152, search 7,014, co-change floor 6,283. Share reaching 80 % within 16k: 66 %, 52 %, 56 %. The medians are on different subsets, but none shows the typed store reaching the same recall in fewer tokens.
assumptions.consequence: The test measured ranking at a fixed spend, not the owner's 'fetch small pieces'. About 0.70 recall for about 8,000 tokens per seed is not small.
assumptions.fix: Make tokens to sufficiency the primary outcome: an agent stop, or a stop rule with a sufficiency check. Report precision and recall at matched tokens, and count carry cost.

assumptions.assumption: The session-lookup set (T5) can be dropped and every task can start from a known seed
assumptions.where: protocol-addendum-4.md item 7; protocol.md §4 (seed = a changed file and symbol; commit message excluded)
assumptions.status: weakly supported as a fairness ruling; it creates a silent assumption that the entry node is known
assumptions.why: The literature says the entry point matters more than the traversal: in LocAgent's ablation, removing the search tool costs 19 points against about 2 for removing graph traversal (verify.txt). Graphify's query path starts with lexical seed-finding. The research itself recommended a lexical entry point (lane-agent-graphs BUILD RECS).
assumptions.consequence: Every arm got a perfect seed. The decisive step from natural language to a node was never measured, and the only real-usage task set was dropped.
assumptions.fix: Add natural-language entry tasks (issue text, first prompt of a session). Give every arm the same tuned lexical or embedding entry. Replay the 139 recorded lookups as screening (lane-evaluation D3).

assumptions.assumption: Question kinds can be answered by programs written per kind
assumptions.where: protocol-addendum-3.md item 19; protocol-addendum-5.md A2; protocol-addendum-6.md item 14
assumptions.status: untested; the token comparison was misread
assumptions.why: The typed side's costs (knowing the schema, writing the query programs) were not counted. Final answers were the same size, 31 tokens against 29.5; the 695 is what search read to get there (refute:claims). 8 of 30 held-out questions needed handling changes after their text was read. Question 40 is answered empty. H4 is inconclusive, interval [-0.060, +0.257].
assumptions.consequence: 31 against 695 shows fewer steps for a caller that already holds the right query. It is not a session saving, and it is the same kind of number as graphify's ratio.
assumptions.fix: Expose one generic tool API from every backend (neighbors, impact, path, explain, search), let the agent choose the call, and count tool-schema tokens in every call's prefix.

assumptions.why: The repo is small (477 code files, about 5,400 nodes) and organised as vertical slices: same-folder padding alone scored 0.72 on TUNE. Index gains are smaller at small scale; graphify's own figures are about 1x on 6 files, 8.8x on code only, 71.5x on 52 mixed files. Mobile seeds rose from 17 % on TUNE to 36 % on held-out, and the whole typed win sits there. Every arm fell 0.06 to 0.17 from tuning to held-out.
assumptions.consequence: The result can under- or over-state graph value elsewhere, and within this repo it depends on the runtime mix.
assumptions.fix: Stratify by runtime. Use fresh commits after the freeze (the 75 held-out commits are spent). If generality matters, add a larger, docs-heavy second repository.

assumptions.assumption: UNNAMED: token cost equals the size of a retrieval answer
assumptions.status: contradicted by the program's own measurement
assumptions.why: Usage is calls x window size; 97 % of context tokens are cache re-reads (TOKEN-BOTTLENECK-2026-11.md). A fetched token is re-processed about 50 times (HARNESS §6). FixFlow's fixed prefix is 47 % of its tokens, about 60k per agent window, about 50k of it tool and connector schemas.
assumptions.consequence: Cuts both ways: a smaller answer saves its size times the remaining calls, and a new graph tool adds its schema to every call. Neither was measured.
assumptions.fix: Measure inside sessions: per arm, report schema tokens, carried tokens, and tokens up to a passing change.

assumptions.assumption: UNNAMED: fetched context is the bottleneck a graph should attack
assumptions.status: weakly supported as a target, but bounded
assumptions.why: Fetched content is 23 % to 27 % of context tokens. The larger levers are the orchestrator window, the fixed subagent prefix and the number of steps. 74 % of fetched tokens went to files that were not edited; whether they were needed is unmeasured.
assumptions.consequence: Even perfect retrieval caps the saving at about a quarter of tokens, before its own costs.
assumptions.fix: State the bound. Test the cross-session form (hot paths read in many windows), where a store could act.

assumptions.assumption: UNNAMED: a single seed is the query shape, and co-change recall stands in for 'what will break'
assumptions.why: Contract, invariant and URL edges were built, but no task asked what a change breaks. Multi-seed and Steiner algorithms, named by the critic, were not built.
assumptions.consequence: The owner's 'connections that will or won't break' were never scored.
assumptions.fix: Add tasks with several seeds, and a break-prediction task with an execution oracle (inject a change and see what fails).

assumptions.assumption: UNNAMED: tuning and held-out data are exchangeable
assumptions.why: Every arm fell 0.06 to 0.17 from tuning to held-out. The rejected configuration S1 scored +0.011 higher, interval [-0.004, +0.026]. The mobile share of seeds doubled.
assumptions.consequence: A configuration chosen on tuning data may not be the best for new work.
assumptions.fix: Use rolling-origin splits and stratify by runtime.

assumptions.assumption: UNNAMED: arm code alone keeps future commits out of reach
assumptions.status: held for parser arms; would fail for an agent
assumptions.why: Every container mounted the live working tree with its full git history. In one outside audit of 731 agent runs (Cursor), 63 % of successful runs retrieved the fix from history or the web.
assumptions.consequence: Any agent arm run the same way would be leaky.
assumptions.fix: Mount a clean export or a bare clone limited to the parent commit; no network; a blind transcript audit.

assumptions.assumption: UNNAMED: model size does not matter
assumptions.where: no model named, because no agent was run
assumptions.why: Graph-tool gains shrink from +17 to 21 points at 1.7 to 4B to 2 to 5 at 32B. A frontier model with agentic grep was not significantly beaten by an index (p = 0.08 to 0.09).
assumptions.consequence: A result with a small model would not predict one with the deployment model.
assumptions.fix: Use the deployment model; report by model if more than one is used.

assumptions.assumption: OWNER'S: stars and headline ratios show effect, and the graph type (graph / knowledge graph / temporal knowledge graph) decides the result
assumptions.why: Graphify's 146,932 stars measure adoption. Its 71.5x is a ratio of two estimates (whole corpus against answer size), with no grading and run once; code-only it is 8.8x. Its code-agent result is n = 6 (ERPNext). Independently, on 177 SWE-bench Lite issues graphify ranked the right file first in 25 % of cases against 32 % for BM25. Graphify has no validity intervals and no history, and its code layer is the same family as ours. No source found shows graph type separates wins from losses (widen/lane-agents.md line 185).
assumptions.consequence: 'Graphify works and ours failed' is not like for like.
assumptions.fix: Run graphify as shipped as an arm, code layer then with document extraction, scored for correctness. Its 'affected' command is the analogue of T1 and has no public measurement. Make each layer (model semantics, summaries, validity) a separately switchable arm.

carries_over: With the same facts and algorithm, SQLite, LadybugDB 0.22.3 and DuckDB with DuckPGQ return the same answers on this repo (shown content identical on 770 of 770 held-out tasks). The engine is an operations choice; H5 timing is still unmeasured.

The fact layer: a deterministic, leak-free build per commit (about 5.3 s per build with three running at once, about 4.1 MB per commit, byte-identical on rebuild, 190 snapshots cached) with typed cross-runtime edges. It is a zero-token base for a temporal or cached-conclusion test.

Typed store against scripted search on co-change recall at 8,000 tokens: +0.076, interval [+0.036, +0.118], holding at 2k and 4k tokens. It comes from mobile seeds (+0.151). Outside mobile it is +0.024 [-0.024, +0.074] against search and +0.001 [-0.051, +0.055] against the co-change floor.

Ranking matters more than hop count. A stored community prior on personalised PageRank gave no gain of 0.05 or more (draws +0.009 to +0.032; T2 -0.037). Unbounded traversal in both directions with degree-normalised ranking was selected; 4 hops did as well.
In a vertical-slice repo, folder structure and co-change history are strong floors (same-folder 0.72 and co-change 0.75 on TUNE) that any method must beat.

On structural questions a typed query reaches the answer in 1 lookup against 2.13, and search read about 695 tokens to produce an answer of the same size (31 against 29.5 tokens). This is an exposure for saved steps, not a measured session saving. F1 was inconclusive.

Reusable apparatus: the sealed tasks; 50 blind-checked questions (now development material); the shared scorer and packer; the cross-check equivalence arm; the held-out lock; the three-refuter process; the removed-document path.
does_not_carry_over: Anything about agent tokens, turns, success or mistakes: no agent was run.
Anything about model-extracted meaning, a document layer, doc-to-code links or contradiction finding, which is where graphify's only independent positive result sits.
Anything about summaries, reports or orientation questions.
Anything about temporal validity, caching of derived conclusions, or invalidation: the facts cost zero model tokens, so caching had nothing to save.
Anything about context a change needed but did not edit, or about predicting what a change breaks: the label was co-change.
Anything about the natural-language entry step: every task was handed a perfect seed node; the session-lookup set was dropped.
Anything about an embedding baseline or live agentic grep: neither was an arm.
Token efficiency: every arm filled its 8,000-token budget (median 7,999).
The '31 against 695 tokens' figure as a session saving: it compares answer size with tokens read, and leaves out schema knowledge, query programs and tool-schema prefix cost.
'Graph against relational' as a statement about graphs: H1 and H2 were zero by construction.
Other repositories or scales, and runtime mixes unlike the held-out one (mobile seeds 17 % to 36 %).
The 75 held-out commits as a fresh test set: they are spent.

arch.summary:
The finished test used a typed property graph built by parsers and git. It had a small deterministic layer over the documents: 20 CLAUDE.md invariants with 90 anchors to code, 529 citations and 1,380 mentions. Time was one snapshot per parent commit plus co-change edges. By the loose definition that is a knowledge graph. It was not a model-built semantic knowledge graph and not a temporal knowledge graph (TKG). It had no cached conclusions, no orientation layer and no agent in the loop.

Graphify is the same kind of graph for code: a tree-sitter graph, built with no model. It adds a model-read layer over documents, Leiden clusters with a report file, and an always-on instruction block with hooks. It is not temporal and stores no summaries. Its 71.5x is a ratio of two size estimates against reading the whole corpus, with no answer graded. Its one agent number on code is 6 questions. The only independent gain found for it is on doc-versus-code questions, which is the layer the finished test left out.

The owner is right on these points:
- The architecture was narrow.
- His library idea (cached conclusions with invalidation) is the only part with a mechanism for large savings, and it was untested. The tested facts cost zero model tokens, so there was nothing to cache.

He is not right on these points:
- Stars are adoption, not evidence of an effect.
- Engines did not differ: three engines returned identical answers on 770 of 770 tasks.
- Traversal speed and a cache over traversal save nothing here, because traversal takes about 1 ms.
- Published TKG numbers are chat-memory scores against putting the whole conversation in context.

Our own assumptions were also weak:
- The label gave no credit for context that was needed but not edited.
- The question side's cost of writing queries was not counted.
- The containers mounted the live tree.
- The code graph aimed at the smaller target. My reading of the FixFlow token records shows the most re-read content is the harness's own design documents: the top 30 paths hold 7.1 % of all tokens, and the 15 documents among them hold 4.9 %.

The strongest honest design has seven layers:
1. A working-tree overlay.
2. The existing structure graph with line anchors, symbol-span hashes, a negative-dependency index and a lexical entry point.
3. Meaning: a deterministic doc layer plus model-read typed claims (invariants, decisions, reasons, hazards), bound to code only by a deterministic resolver.
4. Time: validity by commit ancestry, with invalidation driven by the structure and early cutoff.
5. Cached conclusions: the owner's knowledge-store design, given graph footprints.
6. Orientation: pulled, except a small stable pointer and edit-time invariant warnings.
7. One command-line tool whose answers cite lines.

Ceilings are stated against the measured token spend. 97 % of tokens are re-reads, fetched content is 22.5 to 28.5 %, and the prefix is 47 % of FixFlow's tokens. CLAUDE.md alone is about 5 % of FixFlow's context tokens by my arithmetic, as an exposure. Any knowledge layer is at best the third lever, after capping the orchestrator window and stripping the subagent prefix.

layers.layer: L0 substrate: snapshots and working-tree overlay
layers.what_it_holds: Facts per (commit SHA, extractor version), already byte-reproducible. Plus an overlay for the agent's uncommitted and untracked files: their units hide the base's units, so no visible fact points at a hidden one.
layers.how_built: Git plus the existing extractor (version 59da7b753a4d908e). The overlay follows Glean's stacked-database design. No model.
layers.what_it_saves: Nothing directly. It is what makes every other layer correct while an agent edits: agents work in five worktrees with uncommitted files, so a commit-keyed store is stale on the first edit.
layers.evidence: Own: full rebuild 4.5 to 7 s alone, 5.3 s median at three concurrent, 4.1 MB per commit (build-b/facts-NOTES.md; strong). Glean: about 2 to 3 % indexing overhead for Python, about 7 % larger database, queries under 10 % slower (Meta's own figures; strong as engineering, no token evidence; lane-temporal.md 2.4).
layers.cost_to_build: Extractor work only; seconds per change; zero model tokens.
layers.risk: A one-file overlay must re-run the cross-runtime joins (client URL to route), not only the file's parser. Rename identity is heuristic.

layers.layer: L1 structure: typed code property graph
layers.what_it_holds: Exists: functions, classes, tests, files, routes, tables, columns, settings, migrations, screens, outbox kinds, jobs, slices. 35+ edge kinds, including calls, imports, client-URL-to-route, test-to-route, table read and write, setting reads, enqueue and handler, co-change. 5,464 nodes and 18,875 edge rows at the frozen commit. Four upgrades: (1) a line anchor printed on every answer; (2) content hashes per symbol span; (3) a negative-dependency index (in-edges of a kind into X); (4) a lexical BM25 entry point in SQLite FTS5. Embedding entry would be a separate optional arm. Algorithms by question kind: typed path queries for chains, reverse reachability with a budget per edge kind, personalised PageRank with a co-change prior for ranking, and the repository's own slices as clusters (Leiden only as a diagnostic). The store is SQLite.
layers.how_built: Parsers (Python ast, TypeScript compiler API) and git; no model.
layers.what_it_saves: Lookup steps and fetched tokens on connection, impact and chain questions. A typed answer is a median 31 tokens (40 on the untouched subset), where scripted search read about 695 (819) tokens. That is answer size, not session tokens. Ceiling: connection questions were about 7 % of sampled searches.
layers.evidence:
Own, held-out (build-e/result.json):
- Engines identical on 770 of 770 tasks (strong).
- Typed store against scripted search: +0.076 recall [+0.036, +0.118], only on mobile seeds (+0.151).
- Question F1 0.745 against 0.645, interval [-0.060, +0.257], inconclusive.
- Community prior on PPR: +0.015 [-0.010, +0.042].

Outside:
- Map tools with a frontier agent cut tokens 17 to 39 % with success flat (arXiv 2611.07286; medium; steering confounded).
- Codebase-Memory: about 10x fewer tokens but quality 0.83 against 0.92 (authors grading; weak to medium).
- The entry point mattered more than traversal: LocAgent ablation 19 points against about 2 (medium).
- A pre-registered 170,500-episode study credits the embedding index, not the graph (medium to strong; small open models).
layers.cost_to_build: Zero model tokens; seconds per build; the upgrades are extractor work.
layers.risk: Answers questions sessions rarely ask. Hubs: 73 % of code commits touch a file with reach over 15, so answers need caps and grouping. 11.2 % of held-out reference definitions had no node. Published results show possible losses on edit and test-writing tasks.

layers.layer: L2 meaning: deterministic doc layer (L2a) plus model-read claims bound to code (L2b)
layers.what_it_holds:
L2a (exists): doc, section and doc-id nodes; 529 cites, 1,380 mentions (1,054 low confidence); 20 invariant nodes with 90 constrains anchors. Add a validity check on every citation, because 517 of 1,268 backticked names in the docs do not resolve today.

L2b (new): typed claims read from document sections, commit messages and pull-request bodies.
- Kinds: invariant, decision, rationale, rejected_alternative, hazard, contract, procedure, open_defect.
- Each claim has a statement of at most about 40 words, a polarity, a scope, its source span and blob hash, and its anchors as written.
- Edges: constrains and explains (to code); supersedes and contradicts (as candidates).
layers.how_built: A model reads each section once into a fixed schema (structured output). A deterministic resolver, using the docs extractor's existing anchor rules, binds anchors to structure nodes. An unresolved anchor stays raw and is shown as unanchored (the repository's own raw-plus-resolved pattern). The model never makes a code edge. Cache key: section hash, model and prompt hash. Claim ids come from the span hash plus the normalised statement, to avoid the id churn graphify issue #3004 reports.
layers.what_it_saves: Two things: (a) 'which rule applies here and why', answered in a few hundred cited tokens instead of reading a 41 KB handoff or a 44 KB code map; (b) the reasons in pushed text could become pulled. CLAUDE.md is about 7,400 tokens in every call, about 5.1 % of FixFlow's context tokens if every call carried it (my arithmetic, exposure).
layers.evidence:
For:
- graphify-bench (independent; medium): doc-and-code questions 80 % against 70 % with Sonnet, cost -0.084 USD [-0.180, -0.005]; contradiction hunt 4 of 4 against 2 of 4.
- GraphRAG summaries help whole-corpus sensemaking, but the judging is biased: self-comparison 90 against 10 by answer order; LightRAG fell from 66.70 to 39.06 % after correction (medium to strong).

Against:
- LLM-written repository context files: resolution -0.5 and -2 % (not significant), cost +20 to 23 % (ETH; medium to strong).
- Free summary reuse 22.22 % against 26.26 % (SWE Context Bench; medium).
- Static analysers beat 24 LLMs on call graphs (medium to strong), which is why L2b never makes code edges.
layers.cost_to_build: One model read of the in-scope prose, plus prompt and output. Product docs outside docs/program: 29 files, 73,398 words, about 98k tokens. Commit messages: 38,941 words, about 52k tokens (my measurement). Roughly 2 USD by scaling graphify-bench's 7 USD for 261k words (weak). Incremental per changed section after that. docs/program, where the hot reads are, is much larger and partly untracked.
layers.risk: Extraction errors persist. Docs are partly stale. Prose describes later fixes, so building from the live tree leaks into replays. Build non-determinism. Moving rules from push to pull runs into the trigger problem ('nothing fails, so no lookup starts': 21 cases in 5 families in LIBRARY-PATHWAYS).

layers.layer: L3 time: validity by commit ancestry, invalidation driven by the structure
layers.what_it_holds: For each fact and claim: the commit it appeared at and the commit it stopped holding at, by stable identity. Validity at commit K means 'A is an ancestor of K and B is not', which is a set over the commit graph, not a linear interval. For each claim and conclusion: a dependency set (node ids with span hashes, digests for negative dependencies, the prose source span) and a status (valid, suspect or invalid). Two time axes: valid time (commits) and record time (from the journal).
layers.how_built: A diff of consecutive snapshots by stable id, with git rename detection plus signature similarity for identity. The build-systems policy: when a dependency hash changes, mark dependents suspect; re-run the cheap deterministic check; if the result is equal, re-stamp and stop (early cutoff, as in Skyframe, Salsa and rustc red-green); otherwise invalidate. For model claims a changed anchor means suspect, never false. No model.
layers.what_it_saves: Directly little. It is what lets L2b and L4 be served without stale content, and it lets a resuming agent read 'what changed near X since K' instead of re-reading whole files or documents (unmeasured anywhere).
layers.evidence: Mechanism: Bazel Skyframe, Salsa, rustc and Glean (strong as engineering; no token evidence). Deterministic supersession: MemStrata 0.91 against 0.57 to 0.59, with plain retrieval serving the superseded value 36 to 38 % of the time (single author; weak). Model-decided invalidation does poorly on independent tests: MemoryAgentBench multi-hop at most 7 % for every method, Zep 7 % single-hop (medium). Graphiti's invalidation is a small-model judgment with no check (read in source). No study of temporal graphs for coding agents was found by any lane.
layers.cost_to_build: Zero model tokens; seconds per commit. The storage economy against 190 snapshots (778 MB) is negligible at this size.
layers.risk: Identity errors across renames split or merge histories (unmeasured for code). An unrecorded dependency serves stale answers; file-level invalidation throws away the hits. Dependency recording so far is specified only for the in-memory reference arm.

layers.layer: L4 cached conclusions: the owner's library
layers.what_it_holds: Verified answers and analyses. Kinds: solved problems, traps, do-not-apply rules, impact analyses, flow explanations, decisions with reasons, slice summaries. Each has the question in searcher's words, the answer, evidence spans, a graph-derived dependency set (symbol spans, typed neighbours crossed, negative dependencies), the producer (model, prompt, session), the tokens the derivation cost, and a status.
layers.how_built: Write-through at solve time by the strong model, with a reviewer's refutation pass. An event journal plus a SQLite index. Lazy invalidation with early cutoff at lookup and at phase close. The entry's own check runs before an actionable entry is served. This is KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN-2026-11.md v1.3.1 (commit 6fba000), with footprints upgraded from file blobs to graph footprints. That upgrade covers the blind spot the design itself names: semantic changes outside the footprint.
layers.what_it_saves: Re-derivations not paid. Unmeasured as a rate; single cases run to millions of tokens (a stored design that had cost about 15M helper tokens was reused, LIBRARY-PATHWAYS f07-4 [M]). The library-pathways model, mostly guessed inputs: 1.03 times the ladder's cost at middle values, 0.82 only when much work comes back, reach is high and entries are good [G].
layers.evidence:
Mostly negative or flat on code:
- VibeMemBench: 11 of 12 solver and memory pairings no better than memory off; 160 of 231 failures in the form of the record (medium to strong).
- SWE Context Bench: oracle summary reuse 34.34 % against 26.26 % with none, free reuse 22.22 % (medium).
- The design's own 59 chosen cases break most at match, use, check and afterlife.
- No controlled study of cached model conclusions about code with dependency invalidation exists.
layers.cost_to_build: About 10 to 20 minutes of the solving session per recorded problem (design estimate), a reviewer pass, one capped command per lookup. Design build to the go/stop point: about six sessions (design section 0).
layers.risk: The trigger problem (no lookup starts). Entry quality. Stale service when a later fix silently changes a stored analysis. Look-alike matches. Private details travelling with entries. Placebo-like effects of a tool's mere presence.

layers.layer: L5 orientation: pointer, slice cards, edit-time warnings
layers.what_it_holds:
Three parts:
- (a) A pushed pointer of at most about 500 tokens, stable across commits: which tools exist, when to call them, and that answers cite lines.
- (b) Pulled slice cards of at most about 800 tokens per slice and runtime: entry points, routes, tables, settings, outbox kinds, constraining invariants, co-change partners and open defects. The skeleton is deterministic; an optional model paragraph is stored as an L4 conclusion.
- (c) Event-driven one-line invariant warnings when an edit or diff touches a constrains anchor.
layers.how_built: Generators over L1 to L4, plus a Claude Code edit hook for (c). Clusters are the repository's slices.
layers.what_it_saves: Orientation reads, and the pushed-to-pulled shift. Moving half of CLAUDE.md's reasons out of the prefix is about 54M tokens, about 2.5 % of FixFlow's context tokens (my arithmetic, exposure). The pointer costs about 0.34 %; each 1,000 tokens of schema costs about 0.7 %.
layers.evidence: ETH: repository overviews did not help find files; LLM-written context files raised cost about 20 % (medium to strong). Graphify's report and always-on block have no independent measurement, and advisory text was often ignored (0 graph calls in a 60-session audit; grep against graph 46 to 18; weak). The diff warning under the knowledge-store v1.3 rule would have fired on 48.7 % of 154 commits before the refuters narrowed it (own).
layers.cost_to_build: Generator scripts and one hook; zero model tokens except optional card paragraphs.
layers.risk: Push to pull is the biggest single risk: CLAUDE.md's traps were each paid for, and an agent that does not know a rule exists will not ask for it. Changing CLAUDE.md is the owner's decision and only an arm in tests. Generated content in the prefix breaks prompt caching. Noisy hooks get ignored.

layers.layer: L6 tools: one CLI with capped, cited answers
layers.what_it_holds:
Every answer is typed items with path:line, grouped and capped, with a 'more available' count and explicit unknown or unanchored markers. Target caps per call are design targets, not measurements:
- find: 300 to 600 tokens
- neighbors: 500 to 1,500
- impact: 800 to 2,000 (contracts, tests and invariants across runtimes, grouped by slice; graphify's affected is the analogue)
- rules: 100 to 500
- explain: 200 to 800 (a valid conclusion, else a deterministic card)
- changed --since: 200 to 800
- recall: 2,000 characters, with the entry's check run first
- record: write-through
layers.how_built: A Node CLI called through Bash over SQLite, so it costs no tool-schema tokens in the prefix. A tool server with schemas is a factor to test, not a default.
layers.what_it_saves: Fewer steps and smaller results. Cited lines stop the 'graph answer, then re-read the file' pattern.
layers.evidence: Graphify users re-read files because 82 % of nodes had no source line (third party; weak to medium). The prefix is 47 % of FixFlow's tokens, about 50k of the roughly 60k per agent window being tool and connector schemas (TOKEN-BOTTLENECK-2026-11.md; strong). Recurring choices in tools that report gains: lexical entry, 1 to 2 hop capped expansion, token-capped outputs, a few tools beside grep and read (lane-agents.md section 4; medium).
layers.risk: Agents may not call the tools (adoption from 0 in 60 sessions to 42 % of trials in published work). Caps can drop a prerequisite: fewer tokens with a missing prerequisite is not a win.

arms_to_test: A0: default tools (search and read), parent-era CLAUDE.md. The baseline.
A0p: placebo CLI with an equal-length pointer that returns plausible but uninformative output. Separates the effect of any extra tool and its description tokens from the effect of the content.
A0x: non-graph index. Capped lexical (BM25/FTS) search over symbols, signatures and doc sections, in the same output format as A1. Separates 'an index with capped, cited output' from 'a graph'.
A1: structure layer as a tool (find, neighbors, impact over L1 plus the deterministic doc layer). The finished test's graph, now with an agent.
A2: A1 plus model-read claims bound to code, plus the rules tool and slice cards. Tests the meaning layer.
A3: A2 plus the time layer and cached conclusions, seeded by replaying earlier commits and served with invalidation. Tests the owner's library.
A3s: A3 with invalidation switched off. The stale control.
G1: graphify as shipped, code layer only (tree-sitter, no model), with its own instruction block and default hooks.
G2: graphify as shipped with document extraction by a model. Its one independently measured gain is in this layer.
Factor S on A2 and G2: advisory steering against a forced first query, to separate steering from content.
Factor P on A2: rules fully pushed (today's CLAUDE.md) against one-liners pushed and reasons pulled through rules. Measures the push-to-pull lever and its risk.
Optional E (owner's decision; needs a model download and reverses an earlier 'do not build'): A1 with an embedding entry point instead of a lexical one.

Optional T (owner's decision; needs a graph-database server): Graphiti as shipped, ingesting docs and commit messages, used only on the D4 invalidation test. Model-decided against structure-decided invalidation.

Order:
- D2 break oracle (repo checkers as reference, scripted, no agent) and D4 invalidation replay (no model first), across all arms that apply.
- D3 recorded-lookup screen.
- D5, about 100 fresh questions including doc-versus-code and 'which invariant applies', with all arms.
- D1 replayed commits with a live agent: a 12x4x3 pilot, then about 40 tasks x 3 arms x 3 runs plus placebo.
- Primary outcome: tokens to a correct result in four buckets, with each arm's own prefix counted. Success is a non-inferiority guard only.
reuse_from_finished_test: Facts extractor (build_facts.js, py_extract.py, ts_extract.js, docs_extract.js, git_extract.js; version 59da7b753a4d908e; 28 of 28 self-tests) at C:/Users/User/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/192654871f6b1294/e24f17dc-4aea-4914-a9d1-280a723d620e/scratchpad/hb/graph2/build/facts/. These are L1 and L2a as they stand. Note that this is a session scratchpad: whether it survives is unknown, and copying it somewhere durable is the owner's decision.
The 190-parent facts cache (746 MiB on disk) in the same folder's cache/ subfolder. It is the ground truth for the D4 invalidation replay, because recomputing at the next commit is free.

Task sets and sealed references:
- tasks/tasks.jsonl, parents.txt, tq_questions.jsonl
- sealed/references.jsonl, tq_reference.jsonl
- the two-reader method (tq_writer, tq_second, tq_resolve, tq_agreement.txt)
The 75 held-out commits and 30 held-out questions are spent for their original claims. Reuse them as development material for new label and question kinds, not as a clean final set.

Arm harness: arms/common loader and output format (spec at docs/program/evidence/harness-bottlenecks/graph2/build-b/arms-common-SPEC.md). Keep the SQLite arm as the store, the same-directory and co-change floors as cheap baselines, and scripted search as a non-agent baseline. The LadybugDB and DuckPGQ arms are needed only for the pending timing question (H5), since their answers were identical.

Grader and statistics: the held-out scoring scripts and cluster bootstrap under sealed/grader/heldout/, plus the protocol discipline (hashes before the run, SCORING_STARTED, three refuters, must-not-claim lists, binding wording rules of addendum 6).
The Linux image definition at docs/program/evidence/harness-bottlenecks/graph2/engines-linux/Dockerfile.txt. Fix the mount: export the parent with git archive, no live tree, no .git history.
Token accounting parsers in docs/program/evidence/token-spend/ (per-call, four buckets, counted once per message id), for live-agent arms.

The layer-4 specification: docs/program/KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN-2026-11.md v1.3.1 (commit 6fba000, not on the current branch). It gives the journal, footprints, early cutoff and ancestry validity; its audit KS-0 is still unrun.
open_questions: Target content: the measured hottest reads in FixFlow sessions are the harness's own design documents (the top 30 paths hold 7.1 % of tokens; the 15 documents among them hold 4.9 %). Should the meaning layer cover docs/program, which is mostly untracked and changes daily (121 untracked .md files now), or only the product docs and code?
The real prefix cost of each layer's pointer and tool schemas, measured. And does a CLI through Bash keep tool use as high as a tool server with schemas?
Adoption: will agents call the tools without being forced? Published adoption ranges from 0 calls in 60 sessions to 42 % of trials, and forcing confounds steering with content.
Can tests, mypy strict, tsc and import-linter run at old parents? D1 and D2 need this, and it has not been verified.
Does the history hold enough 'dependency case' changes (an answer changed while its own anchors did not) for D4 to show anything? Count them first.
How many needed-but-unchanged labels exist per commit? If few, D1's premise fails, and that is itself a result.
How non-deterministic is the model-read claim build? Build twice on 10 parents and compare.

Would the owner ever accept moving the reasons in CLAUDE.md from push to pull, given that each trap was paid for? If not, the largest lever (about 2.5 to 5 % of context tokens as exposure, my arithmetic) is off the table.
Does graphify fully parse this stack (Python, TS, TSX, JS) and extract table read and write edges? Installing it, and the pending graph-engine install, are the owner's decisions.
Which agent model is the deployment target? Published structural-graph gains shrink with model size.
Do cache reads count against the plan's limits? This decides whether prefix savings matter to the owner.
Where do fresh tasks come from? Product history on main runs 2026-05-31 to 2026-08-03 (391 commits); a prospective set may be needed.
How often does rename identity fail on this history, and does a failure split a claim's validity?

Even at its ceiling, is a knowledge layer worth building before the two larger levers? Those are capping the orchestrator window (39 to 74 % of cache-read tokens sit past 200k) and stripping the subagent prefix.

refuter.verdict:
The audit is mostly right that the finished test was narrow. It overstates in five places and is wrong in one. It also missed four real flaws.

Overstatements:
1. The engine axis was the owner's own literal request. The protocol (section 1) said in advance that the engines would give identical answers.
2. Co-change was not the only label. TQ (questions answered by readers and checked blind) and T3 (chains named in documents) were built without it, and TQ credits context that is read but not edited.
3. Smaller answers were measured. Recall was scored at 2k, 4k and 16k tokens and as an area under the curve; the typed store won at 2k by +0.070.
4. "Graph type: contradicted" should read "untested".
5. The "+17 to 21 points" figure comes from the superseded v1 of arXiv 2610.33958. The pre-registered version gives +7.7 points for Qwen3-4B, and there embeddings are never below the graph.

Wrong: "perfect retrieval caps the saving at about a quarter". Removing lookup steps also removes window re-reads, which carry 43.6 to 55 % exposure.

Missed flaws:
1. Answers were path-and-signature pointer lists, so the reads that follow them were never counted.
2. The token records that motivate the work are mostly design and document sessions. Every proposed agent test replays product-code commits.
3. H5 never ran, so the engine axis produced nothing at all.
4. The co-change floor is weak on mobile seeds (0.484 against 0.691 on backend). That suggests an untested hypothesis: the typed store helps where history is thin.

On the architecture: most layers have cheaper substitutes. CLAUDE.md is already in the prefix; docs/CODE-MAP.md maps the repo; git log and diff give history; a co-change list ties the typed store outside mobile seeds. The one layer with a large-saving mechanism is model-made cached conclusions. That is exactly where the build-systems early-cutoff argument fails, because re-checking a model conclusion needs a model call. Its own pathway model puts it at 1.03 times the ladder's cost at middle values. The ceiling figures are exposures measured on cache-read tokens.

The evidence for the document layer (graphify-bench) is weak and directional, not medium. Doc-and-code tasks: 20, a 2-task difference. Contradiction hunt: 4 tasks. Haiku 4.5 reverses the sign. The arms differ in skill text, hooks and subagent use.

Graphify's 71.5x is evidence about its baseline (reading the whole corpus), not about any graph architecture.

claims.claim: Audit: the headline axis became the storage engine; the protocol narrowed the owner's question before any arm was built
claims.detail: The engine comparison was the owner's literal request (brief.md: 'a merely self made graph vs a established relational engine is not a fair enough comparison'). protocol.md section 1 stated before any arm was built that identical facts and algorithm give identical answers, and that engines would be scored on speed, size and effort. Fair criticism remains in two places. First, addendum 3 item 13 still labelled H1 'primary', and the grader's headline led with it. Second, H5, the only measure on which engines could differ, never ran: build-e/result.json bench:rewrite proved the bench but did not run it. So the engine axis yielded no information of any kind.

claims.claim: Audit: five pre-run warnings were not acted on
claims.detail: The agent pilot and the embedding arm are listed in the frozen protocol.md section 8 as owner decisions. They were escalated, not dropped silently. Nothing in graph2/ records whether the owner answered. Community summaries with multi-seed algorithms, and labels for needed-but-unedited context, truly got no response.

claims.claim: Audit: 'experiments are all failing' is false because the typed graph beat search
claims.detail: The literal statement holds: H3 is better, +0.076 [+0.036, +0.118]. But the gain is confined to mobile seeds (+0.151). Outside them it is +0.024 [-0.024, +0.074] against search and +0.001 [-0.051, +0.055] against the co-change floor (build-e/result.json refute:claims). On the owner's metric, tokens, nothing was measured: every answer filled its budget and no agent ran. Accurate wording: the test did not fail; it did not measure what he asked.

claims.claim: Audit: co-change is literally the label (truth circularity), and co-change stayed the only label
claims.detail: The T1 label is the task commit's changes. The co-change feature comes from ancestor commits only (protocol.md section 3), and 38 % of targets had never co-changed with the seed (verify.txt). TQ (30 held-out of 50, answered by reading the code, checked blind) and T3 (chains named in documents) use labels built without co-change. TQ credits read-but-unedited context: tests reaching a function, invariants on a file, readers of a setting, change reach. What survives: the primary T1 gives no credit for needed-but-unedited context, and TQ is small (H4 inconclusive, [-0.060, +0.257]).

claims.claim: Audit: 'connections that will or won't break' were never scored
claims.detail: Partial proxies existed: T2 (tests changed with the production change), the TQ 'change reach' kind (question 44: typed F1 0.99 against 0 for search) and 'tests reaching a function'. There was no execution oracle. Correct wording: scored only through edit-history and reader-built proxies, never by execution.

claims.claim: Audit: the fixed 8,000-token budget means the test never measured 'small pieces' (status contradicted)
claims.detail: Recall at 2k, 4k and 16k tokens, the area under the curve and the share of tasks reaching 80 % recall were all scored (grader NOTES). The typed store beat search at 2k by +0.070 [0.029, 0.112]. 66 % of its tasks reached 80 % recall within 16k, against 52 % for search and 56 % for the co-change floor. Small answers cost recall: typed recall at 2k is 0.416. What survives: no arm could stop when it had enough, so tokens to sufficiency were not measured.

claims.claim: Audit: 31 against 695 tokens is the same kind of number as graphify's 71.5x
claims.detail: Both compare an answer's size with what a baseline consumes. Ours used a scripted search that actually ran: it read a median of 695 tokens, and its final answers were 29.5 tokens. Graphify's baseline is the whole 52-file corpus put in context (about 123,488 tokens against about 1,726 per answer, ungraded; review.md, fetched). Our comparison is far tighter. Neither is a session saving.

claims.claim: Audit and architecture: graphify-bench's doc-and-code result (80 % against 70 %) is a medium-strength independent positive for a model-read document layer
claims.detail:
From the fetched README, I downgrade it to weak and directional:
- 20 tasks, so 80 against 70 % is a 2-task difference, with no accuracy interval.
- Sonnet 5 tokens -129k [-325k, +33k] cross zero. Only the cost interval, -0.084 USD [-0.180, -0.005], excludes zero.
- Haiku 4.5 reverses the sign: 75 % against 80 %.
- The contradiction hunt is n = 4, on contradictions planted in a synthetic corpus.
- The author says the graphify arms carry skill text and per-read nudges and never spawn subagents, while the baseline used subagents in about half its runs.
- One repetition per task; the page gives both 65 and 105 as the task count.
- The author: treat direction, not magnitude, as the finding.

claims.claim: Audit: graph type (graph, knowledge graph or temporal knowledge graph) is contradicted as the deciding variable
claims.detail: No source varied graph type with the other factors held fixed. That is absence of evidence, so the status is 'untested'. 'No source found shows graph type separates wins from losses' survives.

claims.claim: Audit and architecture: graph tools give +17 to 21 points at 1.7 to 4B parameters and 2 to 5 points at 32B
claims.detail: lane-graphrag.md line 152 takes this from the exploratory v1 of arXiv 2610.33958 (79,000 episodes). lane-agents.md reads the pre-registered version (170,500 episodes, with a placebo arm): Qwen3-4B grep 0.114, graph 0.191 (+7.7 points), embedding 0.218, and embedding is never below graph. The direction (gains shrink with model size) holds in both. The size of the gain and the credit given to the graph do not.

claims.claim: Audit: even perfect retrieval caps the saving at about a quarter of tokens
claims.detail: Fetched content is 22.5 to 28.5 % of context tokens. But removing a lookup step also removes a full window re-read: lookup-only calls carry 43.6 % (testbed) to 55 % (FixFlow) exposure (architecture.md table, citing the token records). Both are overlapping exposures, so no single cap is established. The architecture states this correctly; the audit does not.

claims.claim: Audit: the live working tree, with full git history, was mounted in every arm container and would leak to an agent
claims.detail: protocol-addendum-6.md item 7 confirms it. Parser arms were protected only by their code (a git archive of the parent), and a check of 10 tasks found no leak. An agent arm needs a clean export, no .git directory and no network.

claims.claim: Missed by the audit: answers were pointer lists whose follow-up reads were never counted
claims.detail: The frozen primary is file granularity in signature form (addendum 4 item 4). An 8,000-token answer is paths and signature lines that an agent must then open. Recall at 8k measures pointer quality. The token cost of acting on the pointers was uncounted for every arm.

claims.claim: Missed by the audit: the workload behind the token figures is not the workload the next test replays
claims.detail: brief.md says this repo's recorded sessions are almost all document and research work: 767 edits with only 10 on product code, and 94 of 1,527 reads on product code. The architecture measures the hottest re-reads as harness design documents (15 documents hold 4.9 % of FixFlow tokens). D1 and D2 replay product-code commits. A win or a null there does not transfer to where this owner's tokens go.

claims.claim: Missed by the audit: a candidate explanation of the mobile win was never stated or tested
claims.detail: On mobile seeds the co-change floor reached only 0.484 recall, against 0.691 on backend seeds (refute:claims). One hypothesis: the typed store helps where history is thin, such as newer code. Untested; offered as a hypothesis only.

claims.claim: Architecture: a graph database does not store connections more compactly, and traversal (about 1 ms) gives a cache nothing to save
claims.detail: Bytes on disk and latency (H5) were never measured for the finished engines. The 1 ms figure comes from the first, rejected test's in-memory JSON graph (HARNESS section 6). The conclusion that speed does not matter survives on other grounds: a model step takes about 6.6 s (brief.md), and the bill is in tokens. Storage size does not enter token cost, so the compactness point is moot for the owner's question.

claims.claim: Architecture: the owner's library (cached conclusions with invalidation) is the only part with a mechanism for large savings
claims.detail: It is a mechanism per case (one reuse avoided about 15M tokens), not a measured rate. The design's own pathway model, with mostly guessed inputs, gives 1.03 times the cheap-model ladder's cost at middle values and 0.82 only in the favourable corner. Outside code evidence is flat or negative: VibeMemBench 11 of 12 pairings no better than memory off; SWE Context Bench free reuse 22.22 % against 26.26 % with none. The larger levers, capping the orchestrator window and stripping the subagent prefix, are not graph features.

claims.claim: Architecture: commit-ancestry validity with early cutoff (L3) lets cached conclusions be served safely and cheaply
claims.detail: Early cutoff works when re-checking means re-running the same cheap deterministic function. Deterministic conclusions here are already cheap: 31 tokens, about one query. The expensive conclusions are model-made, and a changed anchor makes them 'suspect, never false'. Re-checking them needs a model call; not serving them lowers the hit rate. Fan-out (73 % of code commits touch a file with reach over 15) and negative dependencies widen invalidation. 'What changed near X since K' is mostly git log or git diff on a path.

claims.claim: Architecture: model-read claims bound to code by a deterministic resolver (L2b) add meaning cheaply and safely
claims.detail: 517 of 1,268 backticked file names in the docs (41 %) do not resolve, so many claims will be unanchored and cannot be invalidated by structure. The roughly 2 USD build cost is one third-party figure scaled by word count (weak). Build non-determinism is unmeasured. Supporting evidence is weak (graphify-bench). Opposing evidence is medium to strong: the ETH AGENTS.md study found cost up about 20 to 23 % with no success gain.

claims.claim: Architecture: the rules tool, slice cards and edit-time warnings (L2a and L5) save orientation tokens
claims.detail:
Cheaper substitutes already exist:
- The 20 invariants come from CLAUDE.md, which is already in every call's prefix, so a rules answer repeats content the agent holds unless CLAUDE.md shrinks.
- Slice cards overlap docs/CODE-MAP.md Part 3.
- Edit-time warnings need only the 90-row anchor table and a hook, not a graph.

claims.claim: Architecture: moving CLAUDE.md's reasons from push to pull is about 2.5 to 5 % of FixFlow context tokens
claims.detail: This is an exposure on prefix tokens, which are mostly cache reads. Whether cache reads count against the owner's limits is the architecture's own open question 11. Pulled text enters the uncached tail of the window and is re-read on every later call, so pulling often can cost more than the cached prefix it replaced. The risk of a missed paid-for trap is real.

claims.claim: Architecture: the structure graph (L1) as impact and neighbour tools beats reading
claims.detail: Outside mobile seeds the typed store tied the co-change floor (+0.001 [-0.051, +0.055]). A precomputed co-change list from git history is a cheaper substitute there. The pre-registered small-model study credits the embedding entry more than graph tools.

claims.claim: Graphify's 71.5x headline is evidence for the proposed architecture
claims.detail: It is about 123,488 estimated corpus tokens divided by about 1,726 per answer, over 5 generic questions. No answer was graded. Code only, it is 8.8x (16,997 against 1,929 tokens) (review.md, fetched 2026-11-13; weak). Any retrieval beats reading everything, so it is evidence about its baseline only. Independent check (issue 4341, fetched; medium): on 177 SWE-bench Lite issues graphify ranked the right file first in 25 % of cases against 32 % for BM25 (first 5: 38 % against 64 %).

claims.claim: The wider test could look good for the wrong reason
claims.detail:
Ways it could happen:
- Weak baselines: reading every file, padded scripted search, an A0 arm with a weakened CLAUDE.md.
- Tokens without correctness.
- An index built after the answer exists: model layers or seeded conclusions built from the live tree; D5 'which invariant applies' questions labelled from the same CLAUDE.md that L2a is built from; contradictions planted by people who know the layer.
- Uncounted costs: build, seeding, suspect re-checks, subagents (graphify-bench counted the main session only), prefix schemas, reads after pointer answers.
- Confounds from steering and subagent use.
- Forking paths: 11 or more arms and factors against a 3-arm main run chosen from the pilot. Confirm on fresh commits.
- Workload mismatch: product commits against spend on design documents.
- Low power: about 40 x 3 detects only a 12 to 16 % token change.

must_not_claim: Graphify proves that graphs cut tokens 71.5x, or graphify's star count shows that it works.
Our experiments show that graphs, graph databases or knowledge graphs do not help or add nothing.
Our typed graph beat search, stated without all of: on co-change recall, mobile seeds only, against a scripted search, at a filled answer budget.
Typed queries answer questions in 20 times fewer tokens, or 31 against 695 tokens is a session saving.
The finished test measured whether a graph cuts an agent's tokens, turns or mistakes.
A knowledge graph or a temporal knowledge graph would have won, or graph type does not matter: both are untested.
Temporal knowledge graphs are proven to help (Zep, Mem0 and LoCoMo results are vendor-run conversation-memory scores against full context).
Cached conclusions with invalidation will save tokens, or caching does not help: the first is untested; the second was shown only for traversal over facts that cost no model tokens.
A model-extracted document layer is proven to help (graphify-bench: 20 tasks, a 2-task difference, sign reversed on Haiku, arms confounded).
Model-extracted graphs are worse than parser graphs in general (shown only for syntactic relations such as call graphs).
Graph tools give 17 to 21 points, without saying small open models, the superseded v1 of the paper, and that embeddings matched or beat the graph.
A knowledge layer could cut the bill by a quarter, a half or any stated share: these are overlapping exposures on mostly cache-read tokens, not savings.
A graph database stores connections more or less compactly than a relational store, or is faster or slower: H5 was never run.
The protocol ignored the owner's request: it ran the engine comparison he asked for and said in advance that answers would be identical.
The finished test never scored context a change needed but did not edit (TQ did, for 8 question kinds, on 30 held-out questions).
Even perfect retrieval can save at most about a quarter of tokens.
Early cutoff makes cached model conclusions cheap to keep fresh.

design.summary:
Protocol draft written (about 190 lines) for a second test of the owner's actual question. It asks whether a knowledge layer lets an agent on this repository do the same work with fewer total tokens and no loss of correctness, and which layer earns its cost.

Each layer is a switch on top of a real agent baseline: structure (the existing typed graph as a tool), meaning (model-read claims from docs bound to code), time with cached conclusions and invalidation, and graphify as shipped. That turns the owner's "graph vs knowledge graph vs TKG" question into measured contrasts; it is untested anywhere I found.

Verdict rules (yes, no, cannot tell) are fixed in advance:
- The primary outcome is total tokens per task, including subagents, tool descriptions and layer build cost spread over use.
- Correctness against sealed references is a guard.
- Stale answers served is a must-be-zero measure for the caching arms.

The draft starts with two free phases that use no agent and no model calls: a feasibility count, then scripted screens (a break oracle and a cache replay over the 190 cached snapshots).

The agent pilot is estimated at 0.17 to 0.55 billion tokens and the main run at 0.6 to 2.0 billion, against about 2.2 billion for all recorded FixFlow context tokens. All of these figures are my estimates, to be measured in the pilot.

The draft says plainly:
- The finished test did not fail; it did not measure tokens.
- Graphify's 71.5x is a ratio against reading the whole corpus.
- The main run can detect only about a 12 to 16 % token change.
- Results on product-code tasks may not transfer to the owner's real spend, which is mostly design and document work.
design.question_tested: On this repository, does a knowledge layer (structure, meaning, time with cached conclusions, orientation) let an agent do the same work with fewer total tokens (build, update and tool-description cost included) and no loss of correctness, and which layer earns its cost?

tasks.what_it_can_credit: Screening only: whether the needed file is in the tool answer at 2k and 4k tokens, by stratum; decides nothing

tasks.what_it_can_credit: Tokens to a passing change, needed context opened before the first edit, wasted reads, invariants cited

tasks.what: Real production diffs plus scripted small changes (route field rename, response shape, return type, setting key, dropped column); about a third break nothing

measures: Tokens in four separate buckets (uncached input, cache-write, cache-read, output), summed over all model calls including subagents; peak context; tokens added by tool results; tool-description tokens
Layer build and per-commit update tokens divided by the tasks served by that index state, added to each task's total; reads that follow pointer answers counted as the agent makes them
Primary: geometric-mean token ratio against A0, paired by task, 95 % cluster-bootstrap interval
Turns, tool calls, wall time with tool latency shown separately
Tool connected and tool called, per run (adoption)
Correctness against the sealed reference (tests pass, set F1, or rubric); needed-context recall before the first edit; wasted reads
Stale answers served, in every arm; outside set K a stale tool answer that is used counts as wrong
All runs counted in their assigned arm, with a 'tool used' view beside it, marked as non-randomised
fairness_rules: Every index is built from a git archive export of the parent commit, or at the oldest parent and updated commit by commit in order; never from the live tree or a later commit

Agent environment: one-commit export, no .git history, no live tree mounted, no network except the model provider, memory files off, parent-era CLAUDE.md only; a blind transcript audit with a published list of exclusions
Same model, version and effort for every arm; same turn, time and token caps; arms interleaved in time and in random order
Tool descriptions of matched length and style; their tokens count against the arm
Graphify runs as shipped at a pinned version with its own instructions and hooks, not tuned by us
References sealed and hashed before any arm runs; writers never see arm output; no reference produced by an extractor an arm uses; 'which rule applies' questions reported as their own stratum
Tuning split (pilot tasks plus the spent 75 commits and 50 questions) for all choices; held-out split run once after protocol, sample size and thresholds are frozen and hashed
Scoring by script wherever the answer is a set or test result; judge only for rubric questions, shuffled order, human sample; scorer independent of whoever built the arms
Three refuters before reporting; refuter.md's must-not-claim list binds the wording
Model-built layers built twice on 10 parents and the difference reported
Three pre-declared primary contrasts (A1, A3 and G2 each against A0), corrected for testing three; everything else secondary; splits by runtime and task kind are descriptive only

design.estimated_cost:
These are my estimates, assuming 1 to 3M tokens per change-task run and 0.1 to 0.4M per question run, mostly cache reads; the pilot will measure the real figures.
- Phases 0 and 1: zero model tokens.
- Model-layer builds: 0.3 to 1M tokens each, built twice.
- Pilot: about 0.17 to 0.55 billion tokens (144 change runs plus 300 question runs) and 4 to 16 hours of change runs at three in parallel.
- Main run: about 0.6 to 2.0 billion tokens and 15 to 60 hours of change runs.
- For comparison, all recorded FixFlow context tokens are about 2.2 billion (my arithmetic from the token records). The main run alone could cost as much as everything recorded so far.
risks: Low power: 40 tasks x 3 runs detects only about a 12 to 16 % token change, and correctness only as a guard against a large loss; a smaller real effect will read as 'cannot tell'
Workload mismatch: the owner's measured spend is mostly design and document work, while the change and break tasks replay product commits; only Q's document stratum targets his spend
Adoption: agents may not call the tools (published range: from 0 calls in 60 sessions to 42 % of trials); forcing a call mixes up steering and content, hence factor S
Feasibility unknown: tests and type checkers may not run at old parents; the needed-but-not-edited and 'answer changed, anchors did not' cases may be too few
Re-checking a cached model conclusion needs a model call, so early cutoff may not make A3 cheap; the per-case saving is not a measured rate
Model-built layers may be non-deterministic, and 41 % of backticked file names in the docs do not resolve, so many claims will have no anchor
Forking paths: many arms and factors; only three pre-declared contrasts may carry a verdict, and the held-out split runs once
Leaks if any index or agent reaches later commits or the live tree; mitigated by clean exports and a blind audit
Token per-run estimates are assumptions from published SWE-bench traces, not this harness

designCheck.verdict:
The draft is the right shape: a real agent in the loop, every token bucket counted, build cost included, a placebo and a plain-index control, sealed references, invalidation tested first with no model, and the live-tree leak fixed. As drafted, though, it cannot deliver its central promise. The owner's graph / knowledge graph / TKG question gets no verdict, for four reasons:
- A2 is missing from the main change-task run.
- The step contrasts are secondary.
- A3 bundles time validity with cached conclusions.
- No temporal knowledge graph as shipped runs (T is optional and not recommended).

The verdict rules make "cannot tell" likely even for an arm that truly helps:
- The correctness guard passes a truly harmless arm only about 51-64 % of the time (33-47 % if also corrected for three contrasts).
- YES has about 50 % power at the 15 % threshold.
- The under-2 % stale bound needs about 150 or more cache hits, which change tasks cannot supply.

Two rules are wrong as written:
- The phase-1 STOP rule fires on the file-hash policy, which is expected to serve stale answers.
- The CLAUDE.md-invariant reference column would reuse the docs extractor's anchors unless they are rewritten by hand.

Hidden costs and blockers:
- A3 needs the unbuilt knowledge store: about six sessions, half on Opus, behind the owner's own D1/D1b gate.
- The per-run token figure is likely 2-4x low if the real harness (about 60k-token prefix per call) is used.
- No fresh held-out commits exist on main. There are 31 product commits since August on other refs, 27 dated today.

The owner's literal words are only partly covered: spatial topology is undefined, graph-database speed and size (H5) is dropped although free, traversal caching is dropped, and factor P is dropped without saying so.

Each problem has an exact fix in the notes file.

claims.claim: The finished test did not fail; it did not measure tokens
claims.detail: It measured answer tokens (about 31 vs 695) and recall at 2k-16k tokens. It did not measure agent session tokens. Sources: build-e/result.json; refuter.md R6.

claims.claim: Graphify's 71.5x is a ratio against reading the whole corpus
claims.detail: It is about 123,488 estimated corpus tokens divided by the average of five ungraded answers, about 1,726 tokens; it falls to 8.8x on code alone. Weak, self-reported. Source: lane-graphify.md §3.1, from the v8 review.md.

claims.claim: Graphify's one code-agent figure is 6 questions
claims.detail: BENCHMARKS.md ERPNext: n=6, 82.0 vs 70.8 % key-fact coverage, no interval, harness not public (weak).

claims.claim: Independent controlled runs on code with a strong model are flat or negative
claims.detail: Essentially one controlled independent study (graphify-bench: one synthetic corpus, one repetition). The others are anecdotes or a retrieval-only check (issue 4341). On Haiku, graphify saved tokens on code tasks (-119k [-245k, -12k]).

claims.claim: The one independent positive (doc-and-code, 80 vs 70 % on 20 tasks) is weak and directional
claims.detail: refuter.md R8: a 2-task difference; the token interval crosses zero; accuracy reverses on Haiku.

claims.claim: Graphify is a parser graph plus a model-read document layer and is not temporal
claims.detail: lane-graphify.md §1, read from source v0.9.108.

claims.claim: Whether graph type decides the outcome is untested anywhere
claims.detail: Absence of evidence only: no source varies graph type with everything else held fixed.

claims.claim: Making each layer a switch turns graph vs KG vs TKG into measured contrasts
claims.detail: A2 is absent from the main change-task run (arms A0, A1, A3, G2). Step contrasts are secondary. A3 bundles time validity with the conclusion cache. T (Graphiti) is optional and not recommended. Fix: split A3 into A3t (time only) and A3c (time plus cached conclusions), put A2 in the change-task main run, and make the step contrasts primary or label them descriptive.

claims.claim: A0 is the real baseline (how agents work today)
claims.detail: The draft does not say whether A0 may spawn subagents (graphify-bench: subagent use moved the delta from +32k to +107k tokens). With no .git, agents lose git diff. The harness prefix is unspecified (about 60k per call in reality). Fix: give each export a fresh single-commit git repo, give all arms the same subagents, pin the Claude Code version.

claims.claim: Graphify runs as shipped, not tuned
claims.detail: Its post-commit hook finds changes via git diff HEAD~1 (hooks.md, fetched 2026-11-13), and the draft gives agents no .git. Measure G2's build cost from transcripts; one user found graphify's own tracker under-counts subagent usage.

claims.claim: Indexes built from a git archive of the parent cannot see the future
claims.detail: A2's commit-message reads must be limited to ancestors of the parent, never the task commit's own message. A3's seeding must respect ancestry. The replayed-lookup programme documents can only be frozen later than the lookups were recorded.

claims.claim: No reference is produced by an extractor an arm uses
claims.detail: The change-task invariant column would reuse the 90 constrains anchors from the docs extractor that A1 and A2 use. The break oracle's tsc reference overlaps A1's TypeScript compiler API facts. Fix: hand-written anchors; report the oracle by reference source, with the headline on test failures only.

claims.claim: The main run can detect about a 12-16 % token change
claims.detail: Rests on a run-to-run spread taken from one 5-task, one-model study. With YES requiring a point estimate of 0.85 or lower, P(YES) at a true 15 % saving is about 0.50, and about 0.84-0.91 at 20 % (my arithmetic, SE of the log ratio 0.044-0.061).

claims.claim: Correctness against sealed references is a guard
claims.detail: With a paired SE of 5-6 points, a truly harmless arm passes the -10 point guard only 51-64 % of the time, or 33-47 % if corrected for three contrasts (my arithmetic).

claims.claim: For caching arms, the stale rate's upper 95 % bound must be below 2 %
claims.detail: By the rule of three this needs about 150 or more hits with zero stale answers, which change tasks will not reach. Compute it on set K (600 claim-steps) instead.

claims.claim: Phase 1: STOP and fix if any invalidation policy serves a stale answer
claims.detail: The file-hash and whole-repo policies are expected to serve stale answers in dependency cases; that is the finding (lane-temporal.md §5.2). STOP only if a fact-level policy serves a stale answer.

claims.claim: Pilot 0.17-0.55 billion tokens, main run 0.6-2.0 billion
claims.detail: Likely understated. In this harness an agent call averages 113-123k tokens of context, about 60k of it fixed prefix (TOKEN-BOTTLENECK-2026-11.md). A change run is then about 3.5-10M tokens, not 1-3M. The estimate omits A3 seeding, K1, the 90 break-oracle agent runs, sufficiency checks, judge passes, reruns, per-parent dependency environments, engineering builds, owner reading hours and machine or quota contention.

claims.claim: All recorded FixFlow context tokens are about 2.2 billion
claims.detail: 2.13 billion context tokens plus 24.6 million output tokens (TOKEN-BOTTLENECK-2026-11.md).

claims.claim: A3: installs none; build cost is seeding; knowledge-store design v1.3.1 is its specification
claims.detail: v1.3.1 is an unbuilt store of solved defects and traps. Reaching its pilot takes about six sessions, half on Opus, gated by the owner's D1 audit and D1b. The widened kinds and the graph upgrades (span hashes, negative-dependency index, overlay, claim resolver) are new, uncounted engineering.

claims.claim: Held-out change tasks come from fresh commits
claims.detail: Main has 0 product-code commits after a31924a, and all 140 usable historical commits are spent. All refs hold 31 product commits since 2026-08-04, 27 dated 2026-11-13 (my git count). The set must be prospective, with 14 days' wait for the follow-up-fix column.

claims.claim: A2 build costs 0.3-1M tokens
claims.detail: Depends on the route: through harness subagents, every call carries an about 60k prefix. Make the route an owner decision.

claims.claim: Results on product-code tasks may not transfer to the owner's spend
claims.detail: Strengthen it: the document stratum (about 20 questions) cannot carry a verdict, so no verdict is possible on design and document work.

claims.claim: Engine re-testing is not needed because speed does not enter token cost
claims.detail: True for tokens, but the owner asked about a graph database and 'very fast'. The H5 timing and size bench is built, never run, and costs zero tokens. Run it in phase 1.

claims.claim: Factor S separates steering from content
claims.detail: Applies to A2 and G2 only. A1 and A3 have no forced-call condition, so low adoption there reads as 'agents did not use it'.

claims.claim: Arms interleaved in time and in random order
claims.detail: Conflicts with A3's store, which accumulates chronologically. Run 3 independent A3 store chains in commit order and interleave the other arms around them.

claims.claim: The draft covers the owner's asks (graph DB, spatial and temporal topology, caching, invalidation, semantic relations, small and fast)
claims.detail: Spatial topology is undefined. H5 speed and size and traversal caching are dropped. No TKG as shipped runs. Factor P (push to pull) and slice-card orientation from architecture.md §7 are dropped without saying so. Fix: a table mapping the owner's words to measurements (in the notes file, P12).
